title: Ik Khamoshi, Tu Aur Main | Ishq • Fanā • Baqā | SufiPulse USA
description:
IK KHAMOSHI, TU AUR MAIN
Ishq • Fanā • Baqā

An original mystical Sufi kalam written and composed by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Every spiritual journey begins with a distance:

Between the seeker and the Beloved.
Between the ego and the heart.
Between what can be spoken and what can only be experienced.

Ik Khamoshi, Tu Aur Main begins inside that distance.

At first, “Tu Aur Main” — You and I — expresses duality. The seeker longs. The Beloved remains beyond reach. Silence stands between them.

Then the journey turns inward.

Longing becomes remembrance.
Remembrance becomes surrender.
Surrender loosens the boundaries of the self.

What begins as Tu Aur Main approaches Ishq, Fanā and Baqā — Divine Love, the fading of the self-centered ego, and abiding in Divine Presence.

At first, Tu Aur Main is a statement.
Then it becomes a question.
Eventually, even the distinction between Tu and Main becomes too small for what the heart is trying to understand.

“Jo bach gaya… woh Ishq tha.”

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

SufiPulse USA creates sacred media for remembrance, reflection and awakening.

Here, the concern is inward: the distance created by ego, attachment, noise and the illusion of separation.

What remains when the seeker stops defending the “Main” and begins listening for the “Tu”?

Music becomes contemplation. Poetry becomes remembrance. Silence becomes part of the kalam.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

This work is not intended as entertainment alone.

It approaches Ishq, Fanā and Baqā as an inward movement — from separation toward surrender, from self-importance toward remembrance, and toward a quieter awareness of Divine Presence.

It does not define the mystery. It invites the listener to approach it.

Some meanings can be explained.
Others begin only when explanation ends.

title: Take Control | A Ramadan Prayer | SufiPulse USA
description:
TAKE CONTROL – A RAMADAN PRAYER
English & Urdu

An original bilingual Ramadan reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Ramadan is not only a month of fasting.

It is a sacred interruption.

A pause in time.
A recalibration of the heart.
A system reset for the soul.

Take Control – A Ramadan Prayer invites the listener beyond ritual into surrender.

Here, fasting is more than hunger. It becomes exposure. Night prayer becomes intimacy. Revelation becomes alignment. Laylat al-Qadr becomes the mystery of renewal.

“Take Control” is not a demand for power.

It is a plea to be freed from ego so that what governs the heart is not impulse, but intention.

Let Ramadan take control.
Allow yourself to be reset.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

SufiPulse USA creates sacred media for remembrance, reflection, and awakening.

This work approaches Ramadan as structure rather than season.

Ṣawm disciplines appetite.
Tarāwīḥ trains attention.
Iʿtikāf creates distance from distraction.
The Qur’an recalls revelation.
Laylat al-Qadr reminds the seeker that one night can reorient an entire life.

The question is not simply whether we fast.

It is whether fasting changes what rules us.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Ramadan is often measured through calendars, meals, and visible observance.

This work looks beneath the schedule.

Fasting exposes the ego.
Night prayer aligns the heart.
Silence reveals appetite.
Withdrawal prepares return.

The month becomes a spiritual architecture of recalibration.

For the seeker, Ramadan is not exhausted when the moon changes. Its discipline should continue in character, intention, mercy, and self-command.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The language of “reset,” “recalibration,” and “rewrite” is metaphorical.

Laylat al-Qadr is not presented as a mechanical process by which a person controls destiny. The imagery expresses repentance, renewal, surrender, and the possibility of profound spiritual change.

“Take Control” therefore points away from domination and toward surrender.

The deepest control is freedom from the ego’s control.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Aaja Sufi Banja | Step Away From Ego | SufiPulse USA
description:
AAJA SUFI BAN JA
Step Away From Ego

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Aaja Sufi Ban Ja is an inward call.

It speaks to the restlessness that survives beneath ritual, identity, and borrowed certainty.

The work does not reject faith, intellect, or the world.

It asks a quieter question:

What remains when ego steps aside?

The kalam moves gently from fear toward love, from “I” toward silence, from seeking toward being.

There is no demand to perform spirituality.

Here, Sufism is approached as a state of the heart — a movement toward humility, remembrance, surrender, and inward honesty.

Listen without rushing.
Let the pauses speak.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

SufiPulse USA creates sacred media for remembrance, reflection, and awakening.

Aaja Sufi Ban Ja asks what happens when spiritual identity becomes louder than spiritual transformation.

The seeker may inherit the language and symbols — yet the heart can remain restless.

This work turns attention away from appearance and toward condition.

The invitation is not “become someone else.”

It is: become quieter before the truth within you.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The phrase “Sufi ban ja” is not used as a badge, rank, sectarian label, or shortcut to spiritual authority.

It is poetic language for an inward shift.

Step away from ego.
Listen beneath noise.
Allow love to discipline fear.
Allow remembrance to soften certainty.

The composition avoids argument.

Its method is gradual dismantling.

Words recede.
Pauses expand.

The seeker is left with the question that titles cannot answer:

Who are you when the “I” no longer needs to dominate?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

This kalam does not suggest that faith, scholarship, ritual, or intellect are unnecessary.

It questions what happens when any of them are used to protect ego rather than transform character.

Sufism here is an ethical and contemplative orientation, not a claim to spiritual superiority.

The song asks for sincerity before identity.

No spiritual state is claimed for the writer or listener.

The invitation is simply inward.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Nazar-e-Karam Kar De | A Prayer for Inner Elevation | SufiPulse USA
description:
NAZAR-E-KARAM KAR DE
A Prayer for Inner Elevation

An original contemporary Sufi prayer by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This work does not reject the older instinct behind “Lift Karadey.”

It refines the intention.

The prayer begins with a familiar request for mercy, relief, grace, and elevation. But as the kalam unfolds, the meaning of “lift” changes.

From wanting more to becoming right.
From external rise to inner alignment.
From desire shaped by the world to correction shaped by the Divine.

This is not a call for wealth or status.

It is a prayer for peace of heart, humility of ego, light for the soul, patience in hardship, and trust in restraint.

The earlier prayer is not shamed.
It is completed.

Because hearts do not turn by force.
They turn by understanding.

The lift happens within.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

SufiPulse USA creates sacred media for remembrance, reflection, and awakening.

Nazar-e-Karam Kar De asks what elevation truly means.

A person may rise in position and remain inwardly restless. Another may lose status yet gain clarity, patience, and surrender.

The prayer is no longer simply “raise me.”

It becomes:

Correct me.
Steady me.
Soften me.
Illuminate me.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The song deliberately avoids mocking material hopes or earlier forms of prayer.

Human beings ask according to what they understand.

The movement is therefore gentle.

Desire is not humiliated.
It is educated.

The outer request becomes inward. The emphasis moves from what should be added to life toward what should be corrected within the self.

This is refinement, not rejection.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Nazar-e-Karam” is devotional language for mercy, grace, and compassionate regard.

The deepest elevation may be a change in the person who is asking.

Peace, humility, patience, restraint, and trust become forms of rise.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Main Hoon Sufi Researcher | A Reflection for Those Who Study the World | SufiPulse USA
description:
MAIN HOON SUFI RESEARCHER
Kainaat Ki Ayat Reader | A Sufi Reflection for Those Who Study the World

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This is not a devotional song and not a lecture.

It is for researchers, scholars, analysts, scientists, and thinkers who spend their lives studying systems, equations, data, organisms, and cosmic structures.

Modern research asks what can be observed, measured, modeled, tested, and explained.

This work turns one question toward the observer:

Who is doing the observing?

Main Hoon Sufi Researcher explores how inquiry into the universe can also become inquiry into intention, consciousness, wonder, meaning, and the self.

Science measures phenomena.
Sufi reflection asks the seeker to examine the one who measures.

Some read signs in cosmic orbits.
Some in the riverbed.
Some in the depth of the self.

The distance to be crossed may also be within.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

SufiPulse USA creates sacred media for remembrance, reflection, and awakening.

How does intention shape interpretation?
Why does wonder so often precede discovery?
Where does meaning begin when measurement reaches its limit?

The invitation is not to abandon method.

It is to examine the researcher as carefully as the research.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Main Hoon Sufi Researcher does not place spirituality above science or science beneath spirituality.

Scientific inquiry depends upon evidence, reproducibility, disciplined method, and scrutiny.

Sufi inquiry belongs to another register: self-examination, ethical intention, inward awareness, remembrance, and meaning.

Not less science.

A more examined seeker.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Kainaat Ki Ayat Reader” uses Ayat — signs — in a spiritual and poetic sense.

The song does not claim that mystical insight substitutes for scientific evidence or validates an empirical theory.

The “vertical axis” of mind, soul, origin, and purpose describes questions of meaning that scientific method may not be designed to adjudicate.

This is not a scientific proposition.

It is an invitation to reflective inquiry.

Beyond belief.
Into understanding.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Ya Dost | Asma Se Qalb Tak | Divine Names & Responsibility | SufiPulse USA
description:
YA DOST
Asma Se Qalb Tak | Divine Names & Responsibility

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Ya Dost explores the relationship between the Divine Names — Asma — and the human heart — Qalb.

It does not attempt to explain theology. It asks what happens when sacred names move from recitation into responsibility.

Each verse approaches Divine Attributes not as labels to be spoken lightly, but as qualities that should reshape intention, conduct, mercy, restraint, and sincerity.

The composition unfolds in two connected parts. Both are required to complete the intended journey.

Listen to Part One and Part Two in sequence.

Names define belief.
Relationship reveals intention.

The work is not meant to provoke debate. It is meant to invite introspection.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Ya Dost asks whether naming a Divine quality changes the person invoking it.

What does mercy demand from one who speaks of the Merciful?
What does justice demand from one who invokes the Just?
What does patience ask of the impatient heart?

The movement is from Asma toward Qalb — from sacred vocabulary toward lived responsibility.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Ya Dost” is used here as poetic address.

It is not a replacement for the Asma al-Husna or a new theological designation.

The phrase belongs to Sufi devotional poetry, where nearness is often expressed through metaphor.

Creed remains intact.
Poetry expresses devotion.

This work is not designed to provoke doctrinal debate. It is designed to turn the question inward.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Names can be memorized.
Relationship must be lived.

The kalam does not suggest that subjective feeling overrides theology or scholarship. It asks whether knowledge of Divine Attributes carries ethical consequence for the seeker.

The journey from Asma to Qalb is not a theological formula. It is a contemplative movement from naming toward responsibility and recitation toward character.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Haji Naam Mila, Par Badla Kya? | The Journey Ended. Did the Ego? | SufiPulse USA
description:
HAJI NAAM MILA, PAR BADLA KYA?
The Journey Ended. Did the Ego?

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This song is not a rejection of Hajj.

It is a reflection on what is expected to change after it.

Titles do not humble.
Names do not purify.
Only meeting yourself does.

A journey was completed.
But was the inward meeting completed too?

Hajj is sacred.
The Kaaba is sacred.
The pilgrimage itself is beyond question.

Character, however, remains accountable.

This work emerged after witnessing people return from pilgrimage carrying an honored title while anger, dishonesty, arrogance, or moral carelessness remained unchanged.

The song does not judge who went.

It asks what returned.

Hajj was never meant to decorate identity.
It was meant to dismantle the ego.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

SufiPulse USA creates sacred media for remembrance, reflection, and awakening.

Haji Naam Mila, Par Badla Kya? asks whether sacred travel reaches the heart as deeply as it reaches the body.

Some never traveled to Mecca yet lived with humility. Some returned from Hajj quieter, softer, and more accountable. Others returned unchanged.

The question is simple: did the journey change my conduct and soften my ego?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The Kaaba is described here as a mirror.

That is poetic language, not a reduction of its sanctity.

A completed pilgrimage deserves reverence.

A human being still requires accountability.

The sacred journey is honored here precisely because its inward consequences matter. Pilgrimage is not questioned; transformation is.

Listen without defense.
Reflect without comparison.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

This kalam also arose from lived experience.

Dr. Zarf-e-Noori recalls being deceived by a person known publicly through the title Hajji. Trust was extended partly because religious identity suggested moral reliability.

Can a sacred title replace transformation?

May humility reach where ritual has not yet reached.
May the heart bend where the body has traveled.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Zair-o-Zabar ka Jalwa | Qira’at-e-Qur’an That Outlived the Fire | SufiPulse USA
description:
ZAIR-O-ZABAR KA JALWA
Qira’at-e-Qur’an That Outlived the Fire

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This is not a historical defense.

It is a moral mirror.

Zair-o-Zabar ka Jalwa reflects on a difficult paradox in Islamic history: preservation can unfold through imperfect human instruments.

The work moves from the siege and burning of Mecca toward the later discipline of Qur’anic recitation, pronunciation, and transmission.

Mecca was attacked.
Walls were shaken.
Meaning endured.

The Qur’an survived through devotion, precision, memory, structure, and disciplined transmission.

It recalls Abu al-Aswad al-Du’ali (RH) and, later, the controversial authority of Hajjaj ibn Yusuf.

It does not justify violence.
It does not sanctify power.

It asks:

If even fire could not erase meaning,
what have we erased through neglect?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

SufiPulse USA creates sacred media for remembrance, reflection, and awakening.

This kalam turns from historical fire toward inner accountability.

Delay, ego, comfort, and indifference can still damage what is sacred within us.

The song moves from stone to heart, from Mecca to the inner Mecca.

History records the fire.
Revelation preserved the breath.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

This work does not rehabilitate Hajjaj ibn Yusuf or reduce the suffering associated with his rule.

Nor does it assign Qur’anic preservation to one individual.

It reflects on how beneficial outcomes can pass through morally complicated historical actors.

The focus is what endured beyond the instrument.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Zair-o-Zabar” is used here as a symbol of precision, pronunciation, continuity, and disciplined transmission.

This is a spiritual reflection, not a comprehensive history of Qur’anic orthography or recitation.

Its question is inward:

If revelation was preserved with such care, what responsibility do we carry toward recitation, understanding, conduct, and inner life?

O Allah,
we burned our inner home.
We abandoned our inner Mecca.
Restore us with mercy, not illusion.
Ameen.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
KHWAJA MERE KHWAJA
A Devotional Adaptation

A contemporary devotional adaptation presented by SufiPulse USA, with adaptation writing and creative direction by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori.

Inspired by the spiritual memory of Khwaja Moinuddin Hasan Chishti (RA), Gharib Nawaz, this work is inheritance carried through love, service, humility, and remembrance.

It reflects a Chishti ethos in which service precedes speech and devotion is measured not by display, but by what it softens within the heart.

It is also offered in memory of Dr. Zarf-e-Noori’s late father, Ghulam Mohammad Khan.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Khwaja Mere Khwaja is approached here as a bridge between inherited devotion and a new generation.

The purpose is not to compete with the original, but to receive its devotional impulse with humility and carry it forward through a contemporary SufiPulse interpretation.

What matters is not performance.

What matters is whether remembrance becomes character.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

This adaptation is rooted in reverence for Khwaja Moinuddin Hasan Chishti (RA) and the Chishti tradition of love and service.

SufiPulse acknowledges the gracious words shared by Haji Syed Ambar Chishti, received not as praise but as responsibility.

This is devotional transmission and personal remembrance, not a claim of authority over the Chishti tradition.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The emotional center of this adaptation is the writer’s late father.

Dr. Zarf-e-Noori remembers Ghulam Mohammad Khan as a quiet seeker marked by remembrance, restraint, and devotion.

His unfinished spiritual longing became, for the son, a responsibility to carry Sufi expression toward the next generation.

This is personal testimony and remembrance, not theological proof or a public claim of spiritual rank.

May Allah grant him Maghfirat.

title: A-lastu Ki Goonj | Rab Ki Khamoshi Mein Rooh | SufiPulse USA
description:
A-LASTU KI GOONJ
Rab Ki Khamoshi Mein Rooh | The Soul Remembers Its First Call

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

A-lastu Ki Goonj is dedicated to children whose abilities are expressed differently, whose silence may carry meaning, and whose presence can reshape the hearts around them.

This is not a song of pity.

It is a reflection on dignity, design, responsibility, patience, and the mystery of the soul.

Some children speak less, move differently, communicate differently, or experience the world outside familiar expectations.

The work does not ask what is missing.

It asks what we may be failing to perceive.

Some voices are quiet
because they carry light.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

SufiPulse USA creates sacred media for remembrance, reflection, and awakening.

This work honors children, families, and caregivers whose patience and attention are often invisible to others.

It also remembers those still waiting for systems or communities to understand what they need.

The song turns from diagnosis toward dignity.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The title invokes “A-lastu” — the primordial question associated in Islamic tradition with the covenant of souls.

Here, that memory becomes a poetic frame for human worth before labels, comparison, achievement, or conventional measures of ability.

The child is not reduced to a condition.
The caregiver is not reduced to sacrifice.

Both remain human beings carrying dignity.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

A-lastu Ki Goonj is a devotional and poetic reflection, not a clinical explanation of disability, autism, neurodivergence, development, or communication.

Silence should not automatically be interpreted as mystical insight, nor should difference be romanticized.

The spiritual language seeks to deepen compassion without replacing medical, educational, therapeutic, or social support.

The primordial covenant is used as sacred symbolism for dignity, remembrance, and belonging.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Gardish | Rab Ki Khamosh Daleel | The Inescapable Cycle | SufiPulse USA
description:
GARDISH
Rab Ki Khamosh Daleel | The Inescapable Cycle

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

You never arrived.
You never left.
You are in the cycle.

Gardish moves through the turning visible in bodies, systems, history, language, power, nature, and time itself.

Nothing here argues.
Nothing here tries to persuade.

It observes what repeats and points toward what appears to endure beneath the movement.

Across disciplines — physicist, doctor, historian, developer, linguist, citizen — the vocabulary changes, but recurrence remains.

This work calls that contemplation:

Rab ki khamosh daleel.

God’s silent sign.

Not shouted.
Not imposed.
Lived through the turning.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Gardish asks what repeated movement teaches the observer.

Bodies age.
Civilizations rise and recede.
Power changes hands.
Languages evolve.
Systems fail and rebuild.
Seasons return.
Lives move through loss, renewal, attachment, and release.

The song does not present recurrence as imprisonment.

Its deeper question is whether there was ever an “outside” from which existence could be observed independently of the One who sustains it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The word gardish carries several resonances: turning, circulation, reversal, instability, and the movement of fortune.

This composition uses that movement as a contemplative architecture.

What changes?
What repeats?
What appears stable only because we are standing inside the cycle?

The spiritual question begins where description turns toward meaning.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Rab ki khamosh daleel” is poetic and devotional language.

This song does not claim that recurring patterns in physics, biology, history, or society constitute scientific proof of God.

The kalam uses cycles as signs for contemplation — a Sufi reading of dependence, change, continuity, and Divine presence.

“There is no escape from His cycle” is not fatalism. It does not deny human agency, responsibility, causation, or moral choice.

It reflects the spiritual idea that created existence never becomes independent of its Source.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Ye Lakeerein Nahi | Lauh-e-Mehfooz Ki Tahrirein | SufiPulse USA
description:
YE LAKEEREIN NAHI
Lauh-e-Mehfooz Ki Tahrirein | A Sufi Reflection on Destiny

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This is not a song against belief.

It is a song against shortcuts.

For centuries, people have tried to read the future through palms, predictions, astrology, and signs.

Ye Lakeerein Nahi asks a different question:

What if the hand was never meant to tell you what will happen, but to remind you how you are living?

The work moves from fear-based prediction toward tawakkul — trust in God — responsibility, self-witnessing, and inner maturity.

It does not invite the listener to decode destiny.

It asks the listener to stop outsourcing the future to strangers.

Not to read your palm.
To read yourself.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This kalam speaks to those surrounded by instant spirituality, fortune-telling, predictive certainty, and promises that someone else can reveal tomorrow.

Is everything already written?
What does trust in God require?
Where does human choice meet Divine decree?
Why do patterns repeat in our lives?

The song turns these questions inward.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Lauh-e-Mehfooz — the Preserved Tablet — belongs to Islamic theological language concerning Divine knowledge and decree.

This composition does not suggest that palm lines are fragments, maps, or readable copies of Lauh-e-Mehfooz.

The title contrasts the human urge to extract certainty from visible lines with a Divine order that cannot be reduced to fortune-telling.

Faith without superstition.
Spirituality without shortcuts.
Meaning without manipulation.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Ye Lakeerein Nahi, Lauh-e-Mehfooz Ki Tahrirein” is poetic language.

It should not be read as a claim that physical markings on the hand disclose destiny.

The work also does not settle theological debates about qadr, human agency, or the relationship between dua and Divine decree.

Its spiritual position is simpler:

Trust God.
Act responsibly.
Examine yourself.
Do not confuse prediction with knowledge.

Tawakkul is not passivity.
Trust does not remove responsibility.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
SUFI HACKER
Dil Ka Code Reader | For Developers, Thinkers & Seekers

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Sufi Hacker enters the hidden system beneath thought.

Using the language of code, debugging, firewalls, memory, identity, and systems, the work turns technological metaphors inward toward the nafs, intention, habit, and consciousness.

The heart becomes a system to examine.
The ego becomes a firewall.
Old wounds become unresolved processes.
Borrowed identities become legacy code.

But the point is not to mechanize the soul.

It is to ask whether the same discipline we bring to complex systems can be brought to the self.

Main hoon Sufi Hacker — dil ka code reader.

Tonight, the code being examined is your own.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Sufi Hacker was written for people who live between logic and longing, code and chaos, ambition and emptiness.

The kalam asks:

Where is the recurring error?
What process is consuming attention?
Which identity no longer serves truth?
What does the ego keep protecting?

It uses technical language to make self-examination legible to a digital generation.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Debugging the heart,” “resetting the inner OS,” “deleting outdated identities,” and “reading the source code” describe reflection, repentance, discipline, and inward clarity.

They do not mean that consciousness or the soul can literally be reduced to software.

Technology is the vocabulary.

Transformation is the subject.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The phrase “root access to the Divine” is poetic language and should not be understood literally.

No human being gains technical or unrestricted “access” to God.

Within this work, the metaphor points toward surrender, remembrance, humility, and devotional nearness.

Its question is simpler:

Can the person who debugs everything else learn to examine himself?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Needle to Noor | Saada-e-Najaat | Voice for Those Facing Addiction | SufiPulse USA
description:
NEEDLE TO NOOR
Saada-e-Najaat | Voice for Those Facing Addiction

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Needle to Noor is a voice for the Mubtala — the person caught in addiction — and for families carrying fear, grief, silence, and hope around them.

This is not a song of judgment.

It is a call toward life.

Addiction can reduce a human being to secrecy in the eyes of society. This work refuses that reduction.

Life is more important than ego.
Life is more important than shame.
Life is more important than reputation.

Reputation can be rebuilt.
A life cannot be replaced.

The movement is from needle toward Noor — from compulsion toward help, isolation toward connection, and silence toward return.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Needle to Noor was created because addiction is still surrounded by stigma, secrecy, and delayed help.

The work speaks to those struggling, those who love them, and those afraid to speak.

Its message is simple:

Do not let shame become more dangerous than the addiction itself.

Ask for help.
Stay connected.
Choose life first.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

This work does not romanticize addiction or turn recovery into a spiritual slogan.

Addiction can involve medical, psychological, and social factors. Recovery may require professional treatment, family support, and sustained follow-up.

Sufi language here offers dignity, hope, remembrance, and solidarity.

It does not replace clinical care.

The person is more than the substance.
The family is more than the crisis.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

For the first time in this project, Dr. Zarf-e-Noori lends his own voice to his words.

The decision grew from personal grief after losing someone close to addiction years ago.

That memory became a commitment:

No one should be lost quietly because a person, family, or community feared shame or reputation more than asking for help.

“Saada-e-Najaat” is used here as a cry toward rescue, return, and renewed life.

This song is remembrance, solidarity, and responsibility.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
“Needle to Noor” is not just a song.
It is a voice for the Mubtala , the one caught in drug addiction, and a reminder that life is more important than ego, shame, or reputation.

Addiction across Kashmir and the broader world is no longer a hidden issue.
Young lives are slipping away in silence while families struggle between fear and stigma. 

This song was created because the conversations around addiction are still filled with judgment, secrecy, and hesitation, when what people truly need is clarity, support, and dignity. SufiPulse has addressed addiction once before in its early months. Today, with stronger resources, deeper understanding, and a larger community, we return to this subject with more honesty and responsibility.

This song gives voice to those who cannot speak for themselves.
It carries the story of pain, the cost of silence, and the call for return.

For the first time, Dr. Zarf-e-Noori , Writer, Lyricist, Composer, and Music Director,  has sung his own words, a decision shaped by personal grief. Years ago, he lost someone close to addiction. This song stands as his remembrance, and his promise that no one else should be lost quietly.

“Needle to Noor” is a Sufi responsibility, because a Sufi does not only worship God; a Sufi serves humanity. Life Is More Important Than Ego, Shame, or Reputation. Life is the only thing that cannot be replaced. Ego delays help. Shame silences the truth. Reputation can be rebuilt. Life cannot. A responsible society chooses life first. If we value life above our ego, shame, and reputation, we save people before they fall too far.

This is our contribution, our solidarity, and our Saada-e-Najaat
for every youth trying to step out of darkness and every family holding on to hope.

If this song reaches you, stay with it till the last line. Sharing it may become your contribution to someone’s return.

title: Ya Ghaus-ul-Azam | Madad Ban Kar Aaja | Come as My Helper | SufiPulse USA
description:
YA GHAUS-UL-AZAM
Madad Ban Kar Aaja | Come as My Helper

An original Sufi devotional kalam by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Ya Ghaus-ul-Azam is a call from the heart toward Sayyid Abdul Qadir Jilani (Rahmatullah Alayh), remembered across the Sufi world as Ghaus-e-Azam.

The work is built around a devotional distinction:

The help is from Allah.
The waseelah is love.

The kalam does not place any saint beside God or treat spiritual intercession as independent power.

Its language belongs to a devotional tradition of turning through beloved servants of God while keeping the heart anchored in Tawheed.

Madad ban kar aaja.

Come as help in my hour of need.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This work explores devotional language familiar within many Sufi traditions: calling upon a saint as waseelah while understanding Allah as the ultimate source of help.

The purpose is not argument.

It is dependence, love, spiritual memory, and trust.

A seeker does not confuse the means with the Source.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Ya Ghaus-ul-Azam draws on the devotional memory surrounding Sayyid Abdul Qadir Jilani (RA), whose life is associated with scholarship, service, discipline, and remembrance.

Muslims differ in how they understand tawassul, istighatha, and language addressed to saints. This work does not claim to settle those debates.

It states its intention clearly:

Allah is the source.
The saint is not worshipped.
The call expresses love, intercession, and spiritual nearness.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Madad Ban Kar Aaja” is poetic and devotional language.

It should not be read as a claim that any created being possesses independent Divine power.

The writer understands help as ultimately belonging to Allah and the waseelah as devotional relationship.

Classical Islamic discussions of tawassul include differing theological and legal interpretations.

This kalam is devotion, not a legal ruling.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Main Habba Hoon | Meri Kahani Dilon Mein Hai, Kagazon Mein Nahi | SufiPulse USA
description:
MAIN HABBA HOON
Meri Kahani Dilon Mein Hai, Kagazon Mein Nahi

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This is not simply a song.

It is a rebuttal to reducing Habba Khatoon to documents, dates, and arguments over what can be proven.

History asks for evidence.
Poetry asks what memory carried.

Main Habba Hoon gives Habba an imagined first-person voice — not to replace scholarship, but to enter the emotional space archives cannot fully contain.

“Meri kahani dilon mein hai, kagazon mein nahi.”

My story lives in hearts, not on paper.

When intellect becomes noise, poetry becomes resistance.
When history forgets, remembrance speaks.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Habba Khatoon survives in Kashmir not only as a historical figure, but through poetry, cultural memory, longing, landscape, and generations of retelling.

Research matters.
Evidence matters.
But cultural memory also carries meaning.

The song does not ask us to abandon history.

It asks history to leave room for the human heart.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Main Habba Hoon is written as a poetic interior voice.

Habba Khatoon is not literally speaking through this recording, and the work should not be treated as historical testimony.

The first-person voice explores loss, memory, dignity, love, and Kashmir’s relationship with Habba.

The work resists arrogance, not scholarship.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Meri kahani dilon mein hai, kagazon mein nahi” does not mean historical claims are exempt from evidence.

It means a person’s cultural afterlife cannot always be contained by surviving documents alone.

This kalam separates historical proof from poetic remembrance.

Where the archive ends, imagination must still identify itself as imagination.

The purpose is not to manufacture certainty.

It is to preserve intimacy.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Khaaki Banda | Satrangi | Manrangi | Zaat Magar Faani Teri | SufiPulse USA
description:
KHAAKI BANDA
Satrangi | Manrangi | Zaat Magar Faani Teri

A contemporary Sufi adaptation by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Khaaki Banda reflects on ego, identity, mortality, and the dust from which human pride keeps trying to escape.

A person made of dust begins to behave as though permanence belongs to him.

He gathers wealth.
He gathers knowledge.
He gathers titles, colors, and distinctions.

Yet the body remains mortal.

“Khaaki Banda” — the human being of dust — becomes a mirror for the illusion of permanence.

Satrangi.
Manrangi.
Zaat magar faani teri.

So many colors.
So many inner shades.
Yet the self remains mortal.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This adaptation draws inspiration from the timeless Sufi voice of Bulleh Shah (RA) and places that inheritance inside a contemporary soundscape.

Its warning is simple:

Do not confuse possession with permanence.
Do not confuse knowledge with awakening.
Do not confuse identity with essence.

Dust remembers what ego forgets.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Khaaki Banda moves between Punjab and Kashmir as spiritual landscapes rather than competing identities.

Soch Kral, Shamas Faqir, Ahad Zargar, and Kumar Sahib are invoked here as a wider memory of humility and Divine Love — not as one uniform lineage.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

This work is an adaptation inspired by poetry associated with Bulleh Shah (RA).

Dr. Zarf-e-Noori’s contribution lies in the adaptation, contemporary lyrical framing, composition, and creative direction.

“The Dust That Forgot Its Source” is interpretive language.

Whatever colors we wear,
whatever identities we defend,
whatever knowledge we accumulate,
mortality remains.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Agar Mohammad ﷺ Na Hotay | Subtitled in 17 Languages | SufiPulse USA
description:
AGAR MOHAMMAD ﷺ NA HOTAY
If Muhammad ﷺ Had Not Been | A Sufi Reflection on the Light of Muhammad ﷺ

An original contemporary Sufi devotional reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Agar Mohammad ﷺ Na Hotay asks a question at the heart of devotional love:

What would faith and guidance mean without the Messenger ﷺ?

The work answers through reverence rather than argument.

It reflects on the central place of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the believer’s encounter with revelation, mercy, prophetic guidance, and the lived form of Islam.

This is not a rejection of Tawheed.

The path remains to Allah.
The Messenger ﷺ is the one through whom the Qur’an was received, taught, embodied, and transmitted to the Ummah.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This kalam asks what gives religious form its living heart.

Its answer is Muhammadan love.

The Messenger ﷺ is remembered not as a distant historical figure, but as the prophetic model through whom faith became lived guidance.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Devotional poetry often speaks through love, longing, and metaphor.

“Without Muhammad ﷺ” should not be read as diminishing Allah’s absolute sovereignty or independence.

Allah is above all creation. Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is His servant and Messenger.

The composition expresses dependence on the prophetic message and example — never independence of the Prophet ﷺ from Allah.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The phrase “this song is revelation” is used only in the ordinary poetic sense of a deeply felt realization.

It is not wahy.

Islamic revelation is the Qur’an revealed to Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. No contemporary song, poem, dream, intuition, or spiritual experience shares that status.

Lines imagining creation “without him ﷺ” belong to a devotional and mystical register, not an uncontested creed.

This is love expressed through poetry. It does not issue a fatwa or replace scholarship.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: RANGDAY YA-ALLAH | The Color of Return | SufiPulse USA
description:
RANGDAY YA-ALLAH
The Color of Return

An original contemporary Sufi prayer by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

“Color me again, O Allah — before the world paints me wrong.”

Rangday Ya-Allah is a prayer of return.

It speaks to the heart that has absorbed the colors of fear, ego, distraction, and worldly pressure until it no longer recognizes its spiritual orientation.

The kalam asks not for another identity, but for purification.

Color me with mercy.
Color me with remembrance.
Color me with surrender.

The “color” in this work is not outward appearance.

It is the inward condition of the soul.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Rangday Ya-Allah asks what happens when the world colors the self faster than the heart can examine what it is becoming.

Ambition leaves a color.
Fear leaves a color.
Pride leaves a color.
Loss leaves a color.
Love leaves a color.

The prayer turns toward Allah and asks for another coloring — one shaped by mercy, humility, remembrance, and return.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The imagery of Divine color belongs to devotional language in which transformation is described through dye, light, polishing, washing, and illumination.

This composition uses color as a metaphor for inward formation.

The world paints through pressure and imitation.

The prayer asks to be recolored through remembrance.

The movement is not toward sameness.

It is from distortion toward sincerity.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Color my soul” is poetic language.

It does not describe a physical process or reduce the Divine to visible color.

The metaphor points toward spiritual transformation: mercy replacing hardness, humility replacing ego, remembrance replacing distraction, and surrender replacing the illusion of control.

The prayer does not ask to escape the world.

It asks to return without being owned by its colors.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Bulla Ki Jaana Main Kaun | Find Who You Are | SufiPulse USA
description:
BULLA KI JAANA MAIN KAUN
Find Who You Are | A Sufi Reflection on the Self

A contemporary Sufi adaptation inspired by Bulleh Shah (RA), presented by SufiPulse USA.

Who are you beneath your name, religion, nationality, language, profession, reputation, and inherited identity?

Bulla Ki Jaana Main Kaun begins where labels stop being enough.

The kalam does not erase faith, history, or community. It questions ego that mistakes every label for the whole self.

Bulleh Shah’s voice moves through negation:

not this,
not that,
not the identity others assign,
not even the identity the ego constructs.

What remains is mystery.

“Bulla ki jaana main kaun.”

I do not know who I am.

The confession is not emptiness.

It is humility before the One who knows completely.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

In a world divided by religion, race, nationality, sect, ideology, and inherited belonging, this kalam asks:

Who are you before the argument begins?

It asks whether identity has become a wall against another human being.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Bulla Ki Jaana is often heard as a challenge to rigid identity.

This adaptation preserves that inward challenge without turning Bulleh Shah into a slogan for being “beyond religion.”

His poetry emerged within a Punjabi Sufi and Islamic cultural world.

The point is not that belief becomes meaningless.

It is that no social label, sectarian badge, nationality, or inherited status can fully contain the mystery of a human soul.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Who am I?” is treated here as a spiritual question, not a denial of personal, religious, cultural, or civic identity.

The kalam does not claim that all religions are doctrinally identical.

Its movement is inward:

from certainty about others
toward uncertainty about the ego,
from classification
toward self-examination,
from pride in identity
toward humility before God.

Only God knows the human being completely.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
BAS KARJEE HUN BAS KARJEE
Enough Now, Return to the Heart | A Bulleh Shah Sufi Reflection

A contemporary Sufi adaptation inspired by Bulleh Shah (RA), presented by SufiPulse USA.

Bas Karjee Hun Bas Karjee carries the moment when longing stops circling and begins speaking directly.

Enough now.

Enough of distance.
Enough of restless searching.
Enough of the self standing between the seeker and remembrance.

The work moves as a dialogue of longing, surrender, and Divine intimacy.

The language changes.
The ache does not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This adaptation brings Bulleh Shah’s spiritual urgency into a modern listening space without treating inherited poetry as a museum object.

The movement is from excess toward simplicity.

From noise toward remembrance.
From argument toward surrender.
From restless identity toward the heart.

“Bas karjee hun bas karjee” becomes an inward threshold.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

This adaptation does not modernize away its Punjabi roots.

SufiPulse places the inherited voice beside a contemporary sonic language so a new generation can encounter the same spiritual tension.

The purpose is continuity, not replacement. The inherited voice remains visible inside the contemporary form.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

This work is a contemporary adaptation inspired by poetry associated with Bulleh Shah (RA).

Dr. Zarf-e-Noori’s contribution lies in adaptation, lyrical framing, composition, music direction, and contemporary presentation.

“Enough Now, Return to the Heart” is interpretive English framing, not a claim of literal word-for-word translation.

सूफ़ीपल्स
सूफ़ी कविता और संगीत का वैश्विक आंदोलन | SufiPulse USA

SufiPulse USA एक वैश्विक sacred-media platform है जहाँ सूफ़ी लेखक, कवि, गायक, संगीतकार, श्रोता और साधक कविता, संगीत, चिंतन और आध्यात्मिक अभिव्यक्ति के माध्यम से जुड़ते हैं।

यह शब्द से स्वर तक, कलम से रिकॉर्डिंग तक, और स्थानीय विरासत से वैश्विक श्रोता तक एक रचनात्मक यात्रा है।

हर कलम को आवाज़ मिल सकती है।
हर आवाज़ को सही रचना मिल सकती है।
लेखक अपनी रचना लाता है।
गायक अपनी आवाज़ लाता है।
स्टूडियो दोनों को सुनने योग्य रूप देता है।
SufiPulse उस कार्य को दुनिया तक पहुँचाता है।

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

यह प्रस्तुति SufiPulse USA की कार्यप्रणाली समझाती है।

लेखक अपनी कविता या कलाम प्रस्तुत कर सकते हैं। स्वीकृत सामग्री को संपादकीय समीक्षा, संगीतात्मक दिशा और उपयुक्त वोकल सहयोग के माध्यम से आगे बढ़ाया जाता है।

वोकलिस्ट अपनी भाषा, रेंज और शैली के आधार पर vocalist pool में शामिल हो सकते हैं।

जब कोई कार्य production stage तक पहुँचता है, SufiPulse Studio USA रिकॉर्डिंग, निर्देशन, mixing, mastering और release coordination में सहायता करता है।

उद्देश्य है कि रचना अपनी पहचान, श्रेय और आध्यात्मिक संदर्भ के साथ जीवित रहे।

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

SufiPulse स्वयं को बाज़ार से अधिक एक सांस्कृतिक और आध्यात्मिक मीडिया आंदोलन के रूप में प्रस्तुत करता है।

लेखकीय पहचान, source attribution और spiritual intent को संरक्षित रखना production का हिस्सा है।

तकनीक का उपयोग परंपरा को बदलने के लिए नहीं, बल्कि उसे अधिक लोगों तक जिम्मेदारी से पहुँचाने के लिए किया जाता है।

कविता और संगीत scholarship का विकल्प नहीं हैं, और “spiritual science” का अर्थ यह नहीं कि हर रहस्यवादी विचार स्वतः वैज्ञानिक तथ्य बन जाता है।

description:
KORTHAS AYE SANAM
Breaking All Measures of Longing | A Kashmiri Sufi Reflection

A contemporary Sufi adaptation carried by the verse of Nyam Saeb, with adaptation and creative direction by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Korthas Aye Sanam enters longing where ordinary language begins to fail.

Nyam Saeb’s poetry is remembered here as a force that breaks measure, reason, and the illusion of a separate self.

The seeker waits.
The veil thins.
Longing becomes its own form of knowing.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Korthas Aye Sanam brings an inherited Kashmiri Sufi voice into a contemporary listening space without flattening its intensity.

The work asks what remains when longing exceeds explanation.

Nyam Saeb’s verse carries the ache.
The adaptation carries it forward with attribution.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Nyam Saeb is remembered in Kashmir as a poet of deep waiting, longing, and spiritual intensity.

This adaptation approaches his work as inherited Sufi poetry, not historical evidence about his inner states.

Annihilation, storm, and burning belong here to mystical interpretation, not historical claim.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Dr. Zarf-e-Noori’s contribution lies in adaptation, lyrical framing, composition, music direction, and interpretation.

The work does not claim authorship over Nyam Saeb’s inherited poetry.

Its movement is from measured longing toward longing without measure — where identity, time, and language begin to lose their ordinary boundaries.

title: Dapyomas Baelyaaras Yaar Laagav | I Told My Beloved, Let’s Begin a Friendship | SufiPulse USA
description:
DAPYOMAS BAELYAARAS YAAR LAAGAV
I Told My Beloved, Let’s Begin a Friendship | A Kashmiri Sufi Song of Love & Longing

A contemporary Sufi adaptation carried by the verse of Soch Kral (RA), with adaptation and creative direction by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

More than a century after Soch Kral’s passing, the dialogue still feels alive.

Creation whispers.
The Beloved is addressed.
Longing becomes conversation.

“Dapyomas Baelyaaras Yaar Laagav” carries the intimacy of a seeker speaking toward the Beloved not through argument, but through nearness.

I told my Beloved:
let us begin a friendship.

The line sounds simple.
Its spiritual weight is not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This adaptation returns to one of the deepest movements in Sufi poetry: the transformation of distance into relationship.

The seeker does not merely describe love.

The seeker speaks into it.

Longing becomes address.
Address becomes surrender.
Surrender becomes remembrance.

Soch Kral’s kalam carries a distinctly Kashmiri spiritual intimacy — direct, vulnerable, and rooted in closeness to the Beloved.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The language of “friendship” with the Beloved belongs to the poetic vocabulary of intimacy, longing, and devotional nearness.

It should not be reduced to ordinary social friendship.

The Beloved remains beyond possession.
The seeker remains dependent.

Yet poetry allows the heart to speak where formal language becomes too small.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

This work is a contemporary adaptation of inherited poetry associated with Soch Kral (RA).

Dr. Zarf-e-Noori’s contribution lies in adaptation, lyrical framing, composition, music direction, and contemporary interpretation.

“The Eternal Dialogue Between Creator and Creation” is interpretive framing, not a claim that the poem records a literal spoken exchange between God and the poet.

The dialogue is devotional language for longing, prayer, remembrance, and inward response.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Al-Razzāq | Rozi Sirf Tujh Se Hai | SufiPulse USA
description:
AL-RAZZĀQ
Rozi Sirf Tujh Se Hai | A Sufi Prayer for Rizq & Divine Provision

An original contemporary Sufi devotional reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Al-Razzāq is a prayer of dependence.

It returns the seeker to a simple truth:

Provision is from Allah.

Work matters.
Effort matters.
Planning matters.

But none of them is the Source.

The song moves through Qur’anic reflection, Prophetic teaching, and Sufi language to distinguish between the means through which provision reaches us and the One from whom provision ultimately comes.

When one door closes, another may open.
When certainty disappears, tawakkul begins.

Rozi sirf Tujh se hai.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Al-Razzāq speaks to a world where income, markets, employers, governments, and economic conditions can begin to feel like absolute powers.

The kalam gently breaks that illusion.

Human beings seek work, plan, build, trade, and ask for help.

But the heart is not asked to worship the means.

The prayer redirects dependence toward Allah while preserving human responsibility.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

This work does not teach passivity.

Tawakkul is not an excuse to abandon effort, planning, work, or accountability.

Islamic spiritual language about rizq places trust in Allah while recognizing the ordinary means through which provision is received.

“Markets and rulers are shadows” is poetic language.

It means that no worldly system is the ultimate source of provision.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Rizq is written before birth” reflects a traditional Islamic understanding of Divine decree and provision.

The song does not tell the listener to ignore economic reality or personal responsibility, nor does it promise that faith guarantees material wealth.

Rizq can be understood more broadly than money alone.

The spiritual movement is from anxiety toward trust — not from responsibility toward inaction.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
DAPYOMAS BAELYAARAS YAAR LAAGAV
Non-Kashmiri Vocal Adaptation | A New Voice for a Kashmiri Sufi Song

A contemporary Kashmiri Sufi adaptation presented by SufiPulse USA.

More than a century after the passing of Soch Kral (RA), the kalam is carried here through voices born outside Kashmir.

Not as outsiders.

As listeners entering another tradition with respect.

The voice may come from another culture.
The inherited words remain Kashmiri.

This adaptation asks whether sacred poetry can travel across accents, borders, and instruments without losing its source.

“Friendship was the veil…
but my seeking was deeper.”

The Beloved remains the center.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

SufiPulse USA seeks to help Kashmiri Sufi poetry travel beyond Kashmir without becoming detached from Kashmir.

This version deliberately uses non-Kashmiri vocal interpretation.

The purpose is not to replace the native voice, but to explore whether careful preparation, pronunciation, and attribution can allow another voice to carry inherited kalam responsibly.

The accent may change.

The source does not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Cross-cultural performance carries responsibility.

A non-Kashmiri singer performing Kashmiri Sufi poetry should not erase the language, flatten its identity, or present adaptation as ownership.

The source tradition must remain visible.

The vocalist carries the composition, not its cultural origin.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Chosen vessels” is poetic language.

It does not imply spiritual rank, supernatural selection, or authority over the source tradition.

A mystic who “still speaks” means inherited poetry continues through remembrance and performance, not literal communication from the deceased.

title: Yeh Ummat Hai? Ya Khwaab Ka Dhoka? | Forgotten Last Sermon | SufiPulse USA
description:
YEH UMMAT HAI? YA KHWAAB KA DHOKA?
Forgotten Last Sermon | Have We Forgotten What Was Entrusted?

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This work is a cry against forgetfulness.

It asks whether the Ummah can preserve the language of faith while losing the moral weight that faith was meant to carry.

Prayers may rise.
Rituals may remain.
Sacred words may still be repeated.

But what happens when justice weakens, mercy becomes selective, dignity is compromised, and belonging is divided by race, tribe, status, or power?

“Yeh Ummat Hai? Ya Khwaab Ka Dhoka?”

Is this truly the Ummah — or only the image of one?

The song turns remembrance into accountability.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This reflection looks toward the Prophet Muhammad’s ﷺ Farewell Sermon as a moral mirror.

Its concern is not whether Muslims remember that the sermon happened.

It is whether its ethical demands remain visible in conduct.

Human dignity.
Responsibility.
Justice.
The rejection of inherited superiority.
Accountability before Allah.

The work asks what remains of a message when it is remembered ceremonially but not carried into character.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Yeh Ummat Hai? Ya Khwaab Ka Dhoka? is not an attack on the Ummah.

It is internal criticism born from belonging.

The song does not claim ritual is empty. It asks what happens when ritual becomes separated from mercy, justice, restraint, and responsibility.

The sharper the question, the more carefully it must first be turned toward the self.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The Farewell Sermon is transmitted through multiple historical reports, and wording differs across sources.

This song is not a scholarly reconstruction or verbatim rendering of one single text.

It reflects on widely remembered ethical themes associated with the Prophet’s ﷺ final public teachings: dignity, accountability, justice, responsibility, and rejection of superiority based merely on lineage or identity.

Poetry here is reflection.

It does not replace hadith scholarship, sīrah, fiqh, or historical study.

description:
KUMAR GANDERBAL
Qalandar-e-Zaman | Tribute to the Caravan of Sufi Scientists

An original SufiPulse USA tribute written by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori for his spiritual guide, Dr. Ghulam Mohammad Kumar of Ganderbal — Kumar Sahib, Mama Ji, Dr. Kumar Faqeer.

This is not an external biography.

It is the testimony of a disciple whose life, spiritual direction, and understanding of knowledge were transformed through his guide.

The song moves through medicine, natural science, astronomy, mathematics, alchemy, healing, remembrance, Ishq, Fanā, and inner peace.

“Ilm bana zikr, zikr bana jaan.”

Knowledge became remembrance.
Remembrance became life.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

For Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, Kumar Sahib is not merely a respected Sufi personality or an honored teacher.

He is the spiritual guide whose presence altered the direction of his inner life.

The composition traces transformation:

Knowledge becomes remembrance.
Healing becomes service.
Science becomes contemplation.
The seeker moves toward Ishq.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The lyrics move through Uloom-e-Tabi‘at, particles, alchemy, astronomy, mathematics, medicine, and healing.

These are not claims that mystical experience replaces scientific method.

They are poetic stations in a Sufi meditation where knowledge deepens humility, remembrance, responsibility, and wonder.

The destination is not science.

It is transformation.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Lines such as “Kumar ki nigah mein rang-e-Khuda,” “har shifa ka noor tha uske paas,” “Fanā-fi’Llāh,” and “Fanā-fi’r-Rasūl” belong to Dr. Zarf-e-Noori’s devotional testimony concerning his spiritual guide.

They should not be read as empirical or clinical claims.

“Qalandar-e-Zaman,” “Qalandar-i-Kashmir,” “Wali,” and “Dr. Kumar Faqeer” are devotional forms of reverence surrounding Kumar Sahib.

title: Main Silsila-e-Owais Hoon | A Soul-Call | SufiPulse USA
description:
MAIN SILSILA-E-OWAIS HOON
A Soul-Call | A Sufi Reflection on the Owaisi Path

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This is not entertainment.

It is zikr, remembrance, and a soul-call.

Main Silsila-e-Owais Hoon turns toward Uways al-Qarani (RA), remembered for extraordinary love of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ despite never meeting him physically, devotion to his mother, humility, and hidden spiritual stature.

The song asks what it means to belong to a path not built on proximity or spectacle.

Love can travel without meeting.
Recognition can exist without display.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Uways al-Qarani (RA) speaks powerfully to seekers who understand longing without possession.

His story is remembered through service to his mother, love of the Prophet ﷺ without physical encounter, humility, and hiddenness.

The work moves through these themes as spiritual stations:

Khidmat-e-Maa.
Ishq bina deedar.
Hiddenness.
Longing.
Remembrance.

The Owaisi path becomes a language for inward transmission — love received without ordinary physical companionship.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Silsila-e-Owaisi” is used here in the mystical sense associated with spiritual transmission without direct physical meeting between guide and seeker.

This does not mean every inward experience establishes formal lineage, spiritual rank, or authority.

The song distinguishes devotional symbolism from institutional genealogy.

Its concern is connection.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Traditions surrounding Uways al-Qarani (RA) include material of differing historical strength and devotional circulation.

This kalam is spiritual reflection, not a complete historical biography.

References to a cloak, hidden transmission, spiritual reply, or unseen communication belong to devotional and poetic tradition unless independently established through reliable sources.

“Main Silsila-e-Owais Hoon” is not a claim by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori to exclusive rank or formal succession.

It is a confession of longing toward the Owaisi idea: that Divine love can reach across distance, silence, and absence.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Ya Rab Mujhe Rizq-e-Halaal De | A Dua in the Spirit of Iqbal (RA) | SufiPulse USA
description:
YA RAB MUJHE RIZQ-E-HALAAL DE
A Dua in the Spirit of Iqbal (RA) | Give Me Honest Provision, Ya Allah

A contemporary Sufi devotional adaptation arranged and composed by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This qawwali is a living prayer.

Its verses ask Allah for purity, useful knowledge, patience, protection from sin, halal sustenance, steadfastness in worship, and an ending marked by sajda and Divine mercy.

“Ya Rab mujhe rizq-e-halaal de.”

Give me provision that is lawful, clean, dignified, and enough.

The prayer does not ask merely for more.

It asks for what can be received without compromising the soul.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Rizq is not only about income.

It is also about how provision is earned, what it does to character, and whether the heart remains free from dependence on what is unlawful.

This work places halal sustenance beside knowledge, patience, restraint, worship, and accountability.

The seeker asks not only what will I receive, but what kind of person will I become while receiving it?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The composition is presented in the devotional and philosophical spirit associated with Allama Iqbal (RA), where prayer, dignity, discipline, and moral responsibility meet.

The musical treatment is contemporary. The concern is timeless: provision should nourish the body without impoverishing the conscience.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

This release is not a legal ruling on halal or haram, nor a promise that sincere prayer guarantees material abundance.

The kalam is devotional reflection: a prayer for clean provision, ethical livelihood, inward restraint, and the strength to refuse what compromises conscience.

References to a grave filled with Noor and a life ending in sajda belong to devotional hope, not claims about anyone’s guaranteed spiritual outcome.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Teri Mitti... Mera Kashmir | Sufi Anthem for Kashmir’s Soul | SufiPulse USA
description:
TERI MITTI... MERA KASHMIR
A Sufi Anthem of Kashmir, Memory & Belonging

An original contemporary Sufi anthem by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Teri Mitti... Mera Kashmir is a song of belonging.

It moves through Kashmir not as a slogan, but as memory carried in rivers, chinars, snow, food, language, shared devotion, and the tenderness of home.

The refrain is simple:

“Teri mitti... mera Kashmir.”

Your soil.
My Kashmir.

The anthem asks what remains when division is stripped away.

Its answer is not uniformity.

It is shared belonging.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This work draws inspiration from Kashmir’s memory of Lal Ded and Nund Rishi — figures often remembered together as symbols of spiritual continuity across communities.

Jhelum flows through more than one identity.
Chinars shade more than one story.
Snow falls without asking sect, language, or lineage.

The call is toward Ek Kashmir: not erasing difference, but recognizing that difference can still belong to one shared home.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Teri Mitti... Mera Kashmir is not a political map set to music.

It is a cultural and spiritual reflection on belonging.

The Kashmir invoked here is made of landscape, shared food, inherited poetry, coexistence, grief, and affection.

The work resists hatred without pretending history is simple.

Unity here does not mean sameness.

It means refusing to make difference an excuse for dehumanization.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Ek Kashmir” is a cultural-spiritual phrase here: a call toward shared dignity, memory, and belonging across communities.

title: Mansoor! Jala! Mita! Bana! Saja! | Burn Falsehood, Adorn the Soul | SufiPulse USA
description:
MANSOOR! JALA! MITA! BANA! SAJA!
Burn Falsehood, Erase the Ego, Create Truth, Adorn the Soul

An original contemporary Sufi anthem by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Jala.
Mita.
Bana.
Saja.

Burn falsehood.
Erase the ego.
Create truth.
Adorn the soul.

This high-energy composition turns toward Mansur al-Hallaj (c. 858–922), the Sufi mystic, poet, and teacher whose name remains inseparable from the cry “Ana al-Haqq.”

The song asks what must burn within us before truth can become character.

The fire is inward.
The battlefield is the self.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Mansoor! Jala! Mita! Bana! Saja! uses the memory of al-Hallaj as a mirror for courage, ego, suffering, truth, and Divine longing.

Its repeated command moves through four spiritual actions:

Jala — burn what is false.
Mita — erase the tyranny of ego.
Bana — rebuild around truth.
Saja — adorn the soul with what remains.

The anthem turns historical memory into self-examination.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Mansur al-Hallaj was a complex historical figure whose life, teachings, trial, and execution have been interpreted differently across Islamic and Sufi traditions.

This work does not reduce that history to a single slogan.

“Ana al-Haqq” is approached through the devotional language of fanā, where the ego is understood as disappearing before Divine Reality.

The song honors the spiritual symbolism surrounding al-Hallaj without claiming that every interpretation is uncontested.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Burn,” “erase,” “fire,” “blood,” and “annihilation” are mystical and poetic metaphors for transformation of the ego.

They are not instructions for physical harm, self-destruction, or violence.

Likewise, “I am the Truth” is not presented here as a declaration that a human being becomes God.

The composition uses fanā and baqā to explore surrender, self-effacement, and uncompromising spiritual conviction.

Poetry intensifies the image.
It does not replace theology or history.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Sheikh! Sheikh! Noorani (RA) | Father of Sustainable Development | SufiPulse USA
description:
SHEIKH! SHEIKH! NOORANI (RA)
Father of Sustainable Development | A Kashmiri Sufi Vision of Sustainable Living

An original contemporary Sufi environmental anthem by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Sheikh! Sheikh! Noorani turns toward Sheikh Noor-ud-Din Noorani (RA), Alamdar-e-Kashmir, as a spiritual voice of restraint, stewardship, and ecological responsibility.

“Ann poshi teli yeli wan poshi.”

Food will endure while forests endure.

The line becomes the moral center of the work.

The song moves through Kashmir’s forests, Dal Lake, Jhelum, Wular, land, water, livelihood, and the responsibility of the human being standing between inheritance and loss.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

The ecological crisis is not only technical.

It is also ethical.

Water can be polluted by systems.
Forests can be lost through policy.
Land can be damaged through extraction.

Behind each system remains a human decision.

This anthem asks whether Kashmir’s spiritual inheritance can still speak to environmental responsibility today.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Father of Sustainable Development” is used here as an interpretive honorific, not as a formal historical title.

It reflects the ecological significance associated with Sheikh Noorani’s teaching that human sustenance depends upon protection of forests.

The work places that insight beside contemporary concerns about water, forests, food security, ecological degradation, and responsibility to future generations.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

This song does not claim that Sheikh Noorani (RA) formulated modern sustainability science centuries before contemporary environmental institutions.

It draws a spiritual and ethical parallel.

Modern sustainable development uses scientific, economic, social, and policy frameworks.

The Sheikh’s remembered teaching offers a moral principle that remains relevant:

human survival cannot be separated from ecological care.

Poetry creates the bridge.
Science must still do the measurement.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
SUFIPULSE
A Universal Sufi Call | Kashmir’s Voice in Every Tongue

A multilingual SufiPulse USA presentation carrying Kashmiri-rooted Sufi expression across languages and borders.

This work begins with one idea:

A sacred voice does not have to remain confined to the language in which it was first heard.

The words may travel.
The language may change.
The spiritual intention should remain visible.

SufiPulse carries Kashmiri Sufi poetry, music, reflection, and remembrance into a multilingual digital space.

One Sufi pulse.
Many tongues.
One human listening.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

SufiPulse USA began reaching listeners across countries and languages.

That raised a practical and spiritual question:

How can Kashmiri Sufi expression travel globally without losing Kashmir?

The answer was not to erase the source.

It was to translate access while preserving attribution, context, and cultural memory.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Multilingual access is not the same as literal equivalence.

Sufi poetry carries metaphor, rhythm, inherited vocabulary, theology, emotion, and cultural memory that cannot always be transferred word-for-word.

Translation therefore requires care.

The goal is to let each listener approach the same spiritual center while keeping the source visible.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“A universal Sufi call” does not mean all Sufi traditions, religions, cultures, or languages are identical.

Universal here refers to accessibility and human resonance.

Likewise, “Kashmir’s voice in every tongue” is poetic framing, not a claim that one platform represents all of Kashmir or every Kashmiri Sufi tradition.

SufiPulse presents one contemporary, Kashmiri-rooted contribution to a much larger heritage.

title: La Ke Bina Kalima Jhooti Hai | Sufi Reflection on Tawheed | SufiPulse USA
description:
LA KE BINA KALIMA JHOOTI HAI
Without “La”, What Does Tawheed Mean? | A Sufi Reflection on La Ilaha Illallah

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This is not merely a song.

It is a spiritual challenge wrapped in chant.

Every believer knows the Kalima:

La ilaha illallah.
Muhammadur Rasulullah ﷺ.

But this work asks whether the first word — “La” — has actually entered the life of the seeker.

“Lā” is negation.

No false god.
No worship of ego.
No surrender to pride.
No obedience to illusion.

The kalima begins by refusing what cannot be ultimate.

Only then does affirmation become meaningful.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Raaz-e-Kalima turns the declaration of faith into an inward examination.

What does “La” reject inside us?

False honor.
Ego.
Inherited arrogance.
Fear of people.
Attachment to status.
Ritual without surrender.

The song does not question the Kalima.

It questions whether the person reciting it has allowed its meaning to challenge the self.

Start with “La.”

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“La Ke Bina Kalima Jhooti Hai” is intentionally confrontational poetic language.

It should not be read as a legal judgment on another Muslim’s faith, nor as a declaration of takfir.

The phrase asks whether words can become empty when the tongue affirms Tawheed while the heart remains dominated by ego, pride, fear, or false dependence.

The target is hypocrisy within the self.

Not another believer.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The Kalima remains a statement of Islamic faith.

This composition does not alter its wording, replace creed with poetry, or claim that mystical interpretation overrides theology.

Its structure is contemplative:

Lā — rejection.
Ilāha — the false objects of dependence exposed.
Illallāh — affirmation of Allah alone.
Muhammadur Rasūlullāh ﷺ — guidance through the Messenger ﷺ.

Lines involving fanā, Noor, fire, and awakening belong to Sufi devotional metaphor.

Poetry intensifies the experience.

title: Main Habba Hoon | Aaj Ke Habba Hoon | SufiPulse USA
description:
MAIN HABBA HOON
Aaj Ke Habba Hoon | A Modern Reflection on Habba Khatoon & Kashmiri Women

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zeenat Ara and Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Main Habba Hoon gives “Habba” a contemporary voice.

Not one woman.
Not one century.
Not one wound.

The song draws upon the cultural memory of Habba Khatoon and Lal Ded to speak about women still shaped by silence, sacrifice, dowry, unequal custom, broken relationships, and the pressure to endure without being heard.

“Aaj ke Habba hoon.”

Habba becomes a mirror.

The figure is historical.
The questions remain present.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This kalam asks what happens when reverence for women of the past is not matched by dignity for women living now.

We remember poets.
We repeat their names.

But do we hear the daughter under pressure, the mother whose prayer is forgotten, or the daughter-in-law expected to remain silent?

The work turns remembrance into responsibility.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Main Habba Hoon is not a biography of Habba Khatoon and does not claim to reproduce her historical voice.

“Habba” functions as a poetic symbol through which contemporary Kashmiri women speak across generations.

Lal Ded is invoked as part of Kashmir’s wider memory of women whose spiritual and poetic voices survived beyond the structures surrounding them.

It asks why some forms of suffering continue to repeat.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The first-person language is literary.

Neither Habba Khatoon nor Lal Ded is presented as literally speaking through this recording.

References to dowry, divorce, custom, silence, and social pressure address lived social realities without claiming every Kashmiri woman shares the same experience.

The work is reflection, not accusation against an entire culture.

It asks culture to become worthy of the women it celebrates.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
LALLA
Noor Ki Maadar | Har Kashmiri Faqeer Uske Dhoodh Ka Qarzdaar

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Lalla – Noor Ki Maadar turns toward Lal Ded as one of Kashmir’s deepest spiritual and poetic presences.

The work imagines her not merely as a historical mystic, but as a symbolic mother of Kashmiri faqiri — a source of courage, inward freedom, spiritual hunger, and uncompromising truth.

“Har Kashmiri faqeer uske dhoodh ka qarzdaar.”

Every Kashmiri faqeer owes a debt to her milk.

The nourishment is spiritual.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Lal Ded’s voice survived centuries because it refused confinement.

Her poetry crossed household, creed, gender, and institution.

This composition asks how later generations of Kashmir’s seekers, poets, faqirs, and spiritual voices may still carry something of that nourishment.

The song invokes Noor-ud-Din Noorani, Habba Khatoon, Bulbul Shah, Samad Mir, and Dr. Kumar within a poetic caravan of Kashmir’s spiritual memory.

Not as one literal lineage.

As echoes within a shared landscape of longing.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Noor Ki Maadar” — Mother of Light — is an interpretive devotional title.

The song does not claim that Lal Ded literally founded every later Kashmiri Sufi lineage or spiritually initiated every figure named in the composition.

The maternal imagery expresses influence, cultural memory, nourishment, courage, and transmission.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The first-person and dialogic passages are poetic.

When Lalla appears to confront Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, the composition is not claiming literal communication with Lal Ded.

It is an artistic device through which the writer turns her remembered fearlessness back upon himself.

The challenge is inward:

Do not write from comfort.
Do not inherit without responsibility.
Do not praise the fire if you are unwilling to be changed by it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Saaz Mein Bhi Tu Hi Hai | Spiritual Music in Islam | SufiPulse USA
description:
SAAZ MEIN BHI TU HI HAI
Spiritual Music in Islam | A Sufi Reflection on Music, Faith & Divine Presence

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Saaz Mein Bhi Tu Hi Hai enters an old question around sacred sound:

Can music become remembrance?

The song is written as an inward dialogue between a seeker, sound, silence, and the Divine Name As-Samīʿ — The All-Hearing.

The seeker asks:

If my heart is in sujood, what does the instrument mean?

The work does not offer a fatwa.

It examines intention, effect, remembrance, and restraint.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Muslims have held differing scholarly views on music, instruments, singing, samāʿ, and devotional performance.

This kalam does not erase those differences.

Instead, it asks:

What is the intention?
What does the music awaken?
What does it make the heart remember?

The question is not only whether sound exists.

It is what sound does to the soul.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The composition draws upon Sufi traditions of samāʿ, devotional listening, and the remembered beauty of Prophet Dawud’s voice, while recognizing differences in Islamic scholarship concerning music.

“Saaz Mein Bhi Tu Hi Hai” is not a universal legal ruling.

It is a contemporary Sufi reflection expressed through poetry.

The listener is returned to intention, conscience, discipline, and remembrance.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The apparent “reply” of As-Samīʿ within the song is a poetic device.

It is not revelation, Divine speech, or a claim that Allah literally spoke new words to the writer.

Lines such as “every note soaked in love is zikr” belong to the imagined devotional dialogue.

They should not be treated as Qur’an, hadith, or religious ruling.

As-Samīʿ is invoked because Allah is The All-Hearing.

The Divine Name becomes a contemplative frame for sound and silence.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
