title: Yeh Dargah Mera Lahu Hai | Ab Tu Le Is Amaanat Ko | SufiPulse USA
description:
YEH DARGAH MERA LAHU HAI
Ab Tu Le Is Amaanat Ko | A Mother’s Dream to Her Sufi Son

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This work is written in the imagined voice of a mother speaking to her son across memory, devotion, and loss.

Hazratbal is not treated merely as a place.

It becomes inheritance.

“Yeh Dargah mera lahu hai.”

This shrine runs through my blood.

The song moves through family memory connected with Hazratbal and Mo’e Mubarak, maternal protection, Zikr-e-Muhammad ﷺ, childhood remembrance, and the passing of an amaanat from one generation to another.

Ab tu le is amaanat ko.

Now you carry this trust.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

The emotional center of the composition is responsibility.

The mother remembers Hazratbal as prayer, protection, family memory, and love of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

Her son is asked not to inherit status, but remembrance.

The bloodline becomes meaningful only if it becomes service.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The work refers to the Banday family’s remembered association with Mo’e Mubarak at Hazratbal.

Within the composition, this is carried through family testimony, not a complete institutional history.

The song also reflects the devotional practice of tabarruk as understood within long-standing Muslim traditions.

It does not present relics as objects of worship.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Several lines deliberately use visionary and devotional language.

“Written by His Command,” “Muhammad ﷺ chose you,” “the soul of Mustafa is in your pen,” and the naming of Zarf-e-Noori are presented as poetic, dream, familial, and spiritual testimony.

They are not claims of wahy, new revelation, prophetic appointment, or infallibility.

Likewise, the mother’s voice after death is a literary device of remembrance and inner dialogue, not a claim of verified communication from the deceased.

The work is devotion.
It is not doctrine.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Baad Az Khuda Buzurg To Hai | Qissa Mukhtasar | SufiPulse USA
description:
BAAD AZ KHUDA BUZURG TO HAI
Qissa Mukhtasar | A Sufi Reflection on Love, Rank & Devotion

A contemporary Sufi devotional reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

“Baad az Khuda… buzurg to hai… qissa mukhtasar.”

After God, the Beloved holds the highest place — the matter, for the lover, is brief.

This work emerges from a question that has followed Sufi language for centuries:

How far can love speak before analysis begins to police its vocabulary?

The composition turns toward Prophet Muhammad ﷺ through reverence, longing, prophetic nearness, and devotional surrender.

It is not written as a courtroom argument.

It is written as qawwali.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

The song arose after criticism surrounding the phrase “Pehla Sufi Muhammad ﷺ.”

Rather than answer through polemic, the work responds through devotional poetry.

Its concern is whether qualities later associated with Sufi spirituality — remembrance, retreat, tears, surrender, Divine love, purification, and nearness to Allah — can be contemplated through the Prophetic example.

The song answers through love.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Baad az Khuda Buzurg To Hai” is devotional language of rank and love.

It does not place Prophet Muhammad ﷺ beside Allah in divinity, essence, or sovereignty.

Allah remains absolutely One and incomparable.

The Prophet ﷺ remains His servant, Messenger, and Beloved.

Calling Muhammad ﷺ the “First Sufi” is interpretive spiritual language, not a claim that the Prophet historically belonged to a later institutional Sufi order or used that label for himself.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Statements such as “written by His Command” or “the pen moved when the heart was whispered to” are poetic and devotional expressions.

They are not claims of wahy, revelation, infallibility, or Divine authorship.

The line questioning who can “place limits” on the Prophet ﷺ should not be read as attributing Allah’s boundlessness to a created being.

The intent is reverence, not theological equivalence.

Love may speak intensely.
Creed remains intact.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Sufi Ban | Darood Ke Saath Farz Nibha | SufiPulse USA
description:
SUFI BAN
Darood Ke Saath Farz Nibha | A Sufi Reflection on Darood, Duty & Deen

An original contemporary Sufi environmental reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Sufi Ban begins with a simple challenge:

Darood padho.
Farz bhi nibhao.

Send blessings upon the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ — and let that love become responsibility.

The song turns remembrance outward toward Kashmir’s lakes, rivers, wetlands, forests, springs, streets, and shared public space.

If zikr softens the heart, what should that heart do when the land entrusted to us is being damaged?

This is where devotion meets duty.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Wular.
Dal.
Nigeen.
Jhelum.
Wetlands.
Forests.
Springs.

They are living systems on which communities, livelihoods, biodiversity, memory, and future generations depend.

The song asks whether love of sacred tradition can remain credible if everyday conduct contributes to pollution, waste, noise, neglect, and ecological loss.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“This is not a failure of law. This is a failure of tasawwuf” is used as moral provocation, not as a technical diagnosis.

Environmental degradation has legal, institutional, infrastructural, scientific, economic, and behavioral causes.

The lyric turns the question inward:

even where laws exist, what happens when conscience does not?

Tasawwuf here means character, restraint, cleanliness, responsibility, and amanat — not a substitute for environmental science or public policy.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The environmental images are poetic but the responsibility is practical.

A lake “weeping,” a river whose zikr becomes “gutter’s raqs,” or birds whose sajda is obstructed are metaphors for ecological harm, not scientific measurements.

Darood is not presented as an environmental regulation or a ritual formula that by itself repairs ecosystems.

The central proposition is ethical:

love of the Prophet ﷺ should deepen conduct.

Remembrance without responsibility is incomplete.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
MERA WALID WALI THA
Aur Main Us Sabr Ka Sufi Hoon | A Sufi Reflection on Fatherhood, Sabr & Spiritual Legacy

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This work begins with a son remembering his father.

Not through inheritance of title.
Not through inheritance of status.

Through sabr.

“Mera Walid Wali tha.”

For Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, Ghulam Mohammad Khan was more than a parent. He was a quiet spiritual presence — remembered through zikr, patience, restraint, and faith without display.

The son does not say:

I inherited his rank.

He says:

I inherited something of his patience.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Spiritual legacy is not automatically passed through blood or name.

A father may leave memory.
A guide may leave direction.
A life may leave an unfinished question.

But the seeker must still walk.

The song moves from father to son, and from the father’s influence toward Dr. Ghulam Mohammad Kumar of Ganderbal — Kumar Sahib — who became Dr. Zarf-e-Noori’s spiritual guide.

Two G.M.K.s.

One was father.
One became master.

Between them stands the seeker.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Wali” is used here as the son’s devotional description of his father, not as an independently established declaration of sainthood.

Likewise, “Qalandar” and “Mard-e-Momin” belong to the reverential vocabulary through which Dr. Zarf-e-Noori remembers Dr. Ghulam Mohammad Kumar.

Its deepest claim is not inherited rank, but inherited responsibility.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Statements such as “written by His Command,” “the heart was whispered to,” or “destiny wrote a second chapter” are devotional and autobiographical expressions.

They are not claims of wahy, Divine authorship, infallibility, prophetic status, or guaranteed spiritual rank.

“Mera Walid Wali Tha” records how a son understands his father.

“Aur Main Us Sabr Ka Sufi Hoon” deliberately shifts the inheritance away from sainthood and toward character.

The inheritance claimed here is sabr.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Sajda Mohammad Ka Tha | Na Adam Ka | SufiPulse USA
description:
SAJDA MOHAMMAD KA THA
Na Adam Ka | A Sufi Reflection on Adam, Muhammad ﷺ & Divine Command

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

The Qur’anic story is clear in its outward form:

Allah commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam.
Iblis refused.

This work enters the story through a mystical question:

What did Iblis fail to recognize?

“Sajda Mohammad ka tha, na Adam ka” is the song’s poetic answer — not a replacement for the Qur’anic account.

The composition reads Adam’s clay as visible form and the Muhammadan Light as an inward Sufi symbol of prophetic meaning.

The failure is seeing only the clay.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

The song turns the story of Adam and Iblis into a meditation on obedience.

Iblis saw hierarchy:
“I am better than him.”

The seeker is asked to see the deeper danger:

worship without surrender can still leave the ego alive.

Zāhir and bātin — outward form and inward meaning — become a question about knowledge, pride, and obedience.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The Qur’an states that the command was to prostrate to Adam.

Accordingly, “Sajda Mohammad Ka Tha | Na Adam Ka” must be understood as mystical and interpretive language.

It is not a claim that the Qur’anic command literally named Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as the object of that prostration.

Noor-e-Muhammadi appears in some Sufi metaphysical traditions, with differing formulations across Islamic scholarship.

This release presents one devotional reading.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The Noor of Muhammad ﷺ within Adam is presented here as Sufi symbolism, not as an explicit Qur’anic statement.

Likewise, “Azazil loved Tawheed” and descriptions of prophetic light passing through the prophets belong to theological and mystical traditions interpreted in different ways.

Nothing in this work means that Muhammad ﷺ is Divine, shares Allah’s essence, or literally inhabits another human being.

Allah alone is worshipped.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is His servant and Messenger.

Poetry explores the sirr.
Creed preserves the boundary.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
PEHLA SUFI MOHAMMAD ﷺ
Noor-e-Muhammad Se Ibtida | A Sufi Reflection on Noor-e-Muhammad ﷺ

An original Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Pehla Sufi Mohammad ﷺ begins with a devotional proposition:

Before the word “Sufi” became a historical label, surrender, remembrance, purification, solitude, mercy, and nearness to Allah found their highest human example in Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

“Pehla Sufi — Muhammad ﷺ.”

Not as a claim about terminology.

As a claim about spiritual origin.

The path begins with his light.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This anthem asks what later Sufi practice is seeking when it speaks of zikr, fanā, adab, humility, retreat, tears, service, and Divine love.

Its answer turns toward the Prophet ﷺ.

The cave. The night prayer. The tears. The remembrance. The mercy. The surrender.

The song reads these as qualities from which generations of seekers drew their spiritual grammar.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Pehla Sufi Muhammad ﷺ” is interpretive devotional language.

The historical term “Sufi” developed after the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ. This release does not claim that he used that later label for himself.

The phrase means that the Prophetic example is understood here as the foundational human model for the inward disciplines later associated with tasawwuf.

Noor-e-Muhammad is likewise presented within Sufi devotional and metaphysical tradition, not as a universally agreed formulation across Islamic scholarship.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The language of “Noor,” “first Sufi,” and “the pen moved when the heart was whispered to” belongs to devotional poetry.

It is not a claim of wahy, Divine authorship, infallibility, or new revelation.

Nor does “Noor-e-Muhammad” mean that Prophet Muhammad ﷺ shares Allah’s essence or divinity.

Allah alone is Creator and worthy of worship.

Muhammad ﷺ is His servant and Messenger.

Love may intensify the language.
Tawheed preserves the boundary.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Shikwa, Jawab-e-Shikwa | Sawaal, Jawaab Bhi Tu | SufiPulse USA
description:
SHIKWA, JAWAB-E-SHIKWA
Sawaal, Jawaab Bhi Tu | A Sufi Reflection on Iqbal, Question & Divine Answer

A contemporary Sufi reflection from SufiPulse USA.

This work begins where certainty weakens.

A seeker asks not on behalf of a nation, but from within one wounded soul.

Why does sajda feel empty?
Why does zikr echo without consolation?
Why can love burn while Allah still feels hidden?

The composition turns question and answer inward.

“Sawaal bhi Tu… jawaab bhi Tu.”

The question leads toward the Source.
The answer returns the seeker to presence.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Allama Iqbal’s Shikwa and Jawab-e-Shikwa spoke with the scale of a civilization.

This work deliberately does not imitate that scale.

It asks more intimate questions:

What happens when faith remains but certainty trembles?
What happens when prayer continues but feeling disappears?
What happens when the seeker cannot understand the silence?

The song does not resolve every question.

It teaches the seeker to remain within it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The title invokes Iqbal’s Shikwa and Jawab-e-Shikwa as a devotional and literary reference point.

This is not a reproduction of Iqbal’s original works.

Iqbal speaks through a historical, civilizational, philosophical, and poetic register.

This composition uses the shikwa–jawab structure for a personal spiritual dialogue.

The scale changes from Ummah to individual soul.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The “voice of Allah” in this composition is a literary and devotional device.

Lines such as “Main andar hoon… sirf mehsoos kar” are not presented as wahy, revelation, literal Divine speech, or a claim that Allah physically indwells the human being.

They express Divine nearness, remembrance, and inward awareness.

Likewise, “the pen moved when the heart was whispered to” is poetic language, not a claim of Divine authorship or infallibility.

The dialogue is imagined.
The longing is real.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Main Murid Hoon | Meri Rooh Us Ki Nazar Mein Hai | SufiPulse USA
description:
MAIN MURID HOON
Meri Rooh Us Ki Nazar Mein Hai | A Sufi Reflection on Murshid, Murid & Spiritual Gaze

A contemporary Sufi reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

Main Murid Hoon is the language of a seeker standing before his Murshid with nothing left to defend.

Not status.
Not argument.
Not self-importance.

Only surrender.

“Meri rooh us ki nazar mein hai.”

My soul lives beneath his gaze.

The line does not describe ownership of the soul. It describes the murid’s experience of being seen, corrected, and inwardly awakened by a spiritual guide.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

The song moves through recognition, trust, discipline, surrender, fanā, and remembrance.

Its central image is the nazar of the Murshid.

In Sufi vocabulary, nazar can signify spiritual attention, care, correction, and transformative companionship.

The work asks what happens when the seeker stops performing spirituality and allows himself to be changed.

The Murshid does not become the destination.

He points beyond himself.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Murshid ke qadmon mein Noor hai” and “meri rooh us ki nazar mein hai” are devotional metaphors.

They do not mean that the Murshid possesses Divine light independently, controls another person’s soul, or shares Allah’s attributes.

Likewise, “sajda in sound” is poetic language for humility and surrender.

Worship and literal sajda belong to Allah alone.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Statements such as “this song was bestowed,” “the pen moved when the heart was whispered to,” or that the Murshid “transmits” are expressions of devotional experience.

They are not claims of wahy, Divine authorship, infallibility, or revelation through the Murshid.

Fanā here means the diminishing of ego and self-centeredness before Allah.

It does not mean physical destruction or loss of moral agency.

A spiritual relationship should deepen responsibility — not replace it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Main Iqbal Hoon | Main Sawal Hoon | SufiPulse USA
description:
MAIN IQBAL HOON
Main Sawal Hoon | A Sufi Reflection on Iqbal, Selfhood & the Question Within

A contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Main Iqbal Hoon is not a claim of identity.

It is a literary act of entering the questions Allama Muhammad Iqbal (RA) left burning for those who came after him.

Who am I?
What is Khudi?
What survives imitation?
What happens when faith loses courage?

“Main sawal hoon.”

I am the question that refuses to die.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Iqbal did not leave behind poetry that asks only to be admired.

His work confronts the reader with movement, responsibility, selfhood, love, history, decline, possibility, and spiritual awakening.

This composition approaches Iqbal not as a monument, but as a living interrogation.

The listener is not asked merely to quote him.

The listener is asked to answer him.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Main Iqbal Hoon” is a poetic voice, not a literal claim by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori to be Iqbal, inherit Iqbal’s authority, or speak on his behalf.

Descriptions of Iqbal as a wali, faqeer, or spiritual revolutionary belong to devotional interpretation.

Iqbal’s relationship to Sufism, Khudi, Rumi, Islamic thought, and modernity is complex.

This work enters that complexity through reverence.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Phrases such as “Iqbal’s words were prophetic,” “the song was whispered,” or “the pen moved when the heart was whispered to” are poetic expressions.

They do not mean prophecy, wahy, Divine authorship, or infallibility.

Prophethood in Islam culminates with Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

The line “Iqbal’s poetry begins where fiqh ends, and fanā begins” is also devotional metaphor, not a dismissal of fiqh or Islamic scholarship.

It distinguishes legal discourse from the inward questions poetry can awaken.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Manzil-e-Maqām | Labbaik Ya Rabb | A Sufi Soul of a Traveler | SufiPulse USA
description:
MANZIL-E-MAQĀM
Labbaik Ya Rabb | A Sufi Journey of Calling, Travel & Return

An original contemporary Sufi travel reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Manzil-e-Maqām begins on the road.

Thirty-two American states.
Seven years.
One continuing search.

The journey turns highways, weather, distance, solitude, and changing landscapes into an inward map.

Every road becomes a maqām.
Every silence becomes an invitation to listen.

“Labbaik Ya Rabb.”

Here I am, my Lord.

The traveler moves outward while asking whether the real destination is within.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Travel changes scale.

Mountains can reduce the ego.
Snow can teach patience.
Waterfalls can suggest return.
Open roads can expose the crowded inner life.

The composition translates years of movement into Sufi metaphor:

from nafs to fanā,
from noise to zikr,
from analysis to surrender,
from distance to return.

The road is physical.

The journey is also inward.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Every weather is a Divine sign” and “every road is a maqām” are contemplative expressions.

The song does not claim that landscapes carry private revelation or that ordinary travel automatically produces spiritual rank.

Maqām, in classical Sufi vocabulary, refers to a spiritual station reached through discipline and transformation.

Here, the word is also used poetically to map stages of an interior journey onto movement through place.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Labbaik Ya Rabb” is used as a devotional response to Allah — a declaration of readiness, surrender, and return.

It should not be confused with a claim that the traveler received a new Divine command or revelation.

The movement from “science to surrender” does not reject science.

It describes a personal transition from measuring the external world to confronting what measurement alone cannot settle: meaning, mortality, longing, and the self.

The road provides the imagery.
The seeker supplies the question.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Har Daur Ka Karbala | Aur Tu? | Every Era Has Its Karbala | SufiPulse USA
description:
HAR DAUR KA KARBALA
Aur Tu? | A Sufi Reflection on Courage, Truth & Karbala

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Karbala was a historical event.

But its moral question did not end there.

Har Daur Ka Karbala turns toward the choices that return in every age:

truth or convenience,
courage or silence,
dignity or submission to injustice.

“Aur tu?”

And you?

The song does not ask where you would have stood in history.

It asks where you stand when the cost of truth reaches your own life.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Karbala remains one of the most powerful moral memories in Islam.

Imam Husain (RA) and those who stood with him are remembered through sacrifice, fidelity, courage, and refusal to surrender conscience.

This work brings that memory into ordinary human situations:

homes,
workplaces,
institutions,
relationships,
and systems.

The battlefield becomes metaphor.

The decision remains real.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Every era has its Karbala” is poetic and ethical language.

It does not mean every conflict, political dispute, personal disagreement, or injustice is historically equivalent to Karbala.

Nor should the symbolism be used casually to declare living opponents “Yazid.”

The purpose is self-examination before accusation.

Karbala becomes a mirror for courage, conscience, power, and moral choice.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

This nazm is not a retelling of the events of 680 CE and does not replace historical, theological, or sectarian scholarship on Karbala.

Its question is inward:

What happens when truth becomes costly?

“Are we Husain — or Yazid?” is a moral metaphor, not a claim that individuals today inherit the sacred rank of Imam Husain (RA) or the historical identity of Yazid.

The work asks the listener to examine conduct before judging others.

You are not being asked to reenact Karbala.

You are being asked whether your conscience survives the test.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Main Bilal Hoon | Mera Aansu Azaan Ban Gaya | SufiPulse USA
description:
MAIN BILAL HOON
Mera Aansu Azaan Ban Gaya | A Slave in Chains, A Voice Islam Never Forgot

A contemporary Sufi reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

Main Bilal Hoon enters the story of Sayyiduna Bilal ibn Rabah (RA) through a first-person poetic voice.

An enslaved African man.
A believer tortured for Tawheed.
A voice chosen for the Adhan.

“Mera aansu azaan ban gaya.”

My tear became the call to prayer.

The line turns suffering into witness.

Bilal’s chains could restrain the body.

They could not command the heart.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Bilal ibn Rabah (RA) stands among the earliest and most beloved Companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

Islamic tradition remembers his endurance under persecution, his declaration of Allah’s Oneness, his emancipation through Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA), and his service as the Prophet’s muezzin.

This composition asks what happens when a voice once treated as powerless becomes entrusted with calling a community to prayer.

The answer is about dignity.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Main Bilal Hoon is dramatic devotional poetry, not Bilal ibn Rabah’s literal speech.

The song uses chains, burning sand, tears, and the Adhan as symbols of faith surviving oppression.

Reports concerning Bilal’s life after the Prophet’s ﷺ death, including later Adhan narratives, vary in historical strength.

The composition treats those scenes as devotional memory rather than uncontested biography.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Mera aansu azaan ban gaya” is poetic.

It does not claim that Bilal’s tears literally became the Adhan.

References to his footsteps being heard in Paradise derive from a well-known hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ told Bilal that he had heard his footsteps before him in Paradise.

The song does not make race itself a spiritual rank.

Its emphasis is that slavery, status, lineage, and racial prejudice could not diminish Bilal’s dignity before Allah.

His story rebukes every hierarchy that mistakes human power for human worth.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Ya Ali, Ya Ali, Ya Ali | When the Soul Calls Its Master | SufiPulse USA
description:
YA ALI, YA ALI, YA ALI
Bab-e-Wilayat | Door of the Sufi World

A contemporary Sufi devotional reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

Ya Ali, Ya Ali, Ya Ali is a cry of love, courage, remembrance, and spiritual inheritance.

It turns toward Sayyiduna Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) — cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, husband of Sayyida Fatima (RA), father of Hasan and Husain (RA), and one of the central figures of Islamic spiritual memory.

“Ya Ali.”

The repetition is devotional remembrance directed toward a beloved servant of Allah.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Across many Sufi traditions, Ali (RA) occupies a foundational place in spiritual teaching, courage, knowledge, adab, and love of the Prophet ﷺ.

This composition approaches him as Bab-e-Wilayat — a devotional image through which generations of seekers understand spiritual chivalry, loyalty, sacrifice, and inward strength.

The song asks what the name “Ali” awakens:

courage without arrogance,
strength without cruelty,
knowledge without pride,
and love without self-worship.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Bab-e-Wilayat,” “Door of the Sufi World,” and descriptions linking Ali (RA) to later Sufi spiritual inheritance belong to devotional and historical interpretation.

This release does not attempt to settle Sunni-Shia theological differences or make one devotional formulation binding upon all Muslims.

It honors Ali (RA) through Sufi poetic language while preserving Tawheed.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Lines such as “har Sufi ki pehli saans Ya Ali,” “Ali ka naam har Loh-e-Mahfooz par likha hai,” or descriptions of Ali as present in every seeker are poetic expressions, not literal doctrinal claims.

Likewise, calling “Ya Ali” in this composition is presented within devotional Sufi language and does not assign independent Divine power to Ali (RA).

Allah alone is worshipped and possesses absolute power.

Ali (RA) is honored as a servant of Allah, member of Ahl al-Bayt, Companion of the Prophet ﷺ, and towering figure of Islamic spirituality.

Love may be intense.
Tawheed remains absolute.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Main Hoon Sufi Tabeeb | Healing Body and Soul | SufiPulse USA
description:
MAIN HOON SUFI TABEEB
Healing Body and Soul | A Sufi Reflection on Medicine, Mercy & the Inner Life

An original Sufi reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

Main Hoon Sufi Tabeeb begins with a healer confronting the first patient he cannot escape:

himself.

The song asks what remains of medicine when knowledge is separated from mercy, or healing becomes only transaction.

“Dard padhta hoon.
Rooh sunta hoon.
Aur shifa sirf Allah se maangta hoon.”

The physician treats.
The seeker prays.
Healing belongs to Allah.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

The composition honors those who care for bodies without forgetting the dignity, fear, grief, and spiritual life of the person inside them.

Its language moves through medicine, zikr, sabr, service, conscience, and ethical restraint.

The “Sufi Tabeeb” is not a supernatural healer.

He is an image of the practitioner who asks whether professional skill has also produced humility.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

This work is inspired by the spiritual influence of Dr. Ghulam Mohammad Kumar of Ganderbal — Kumar Sahib — and pays tribute to Dr. Mushtaq as a physician and seeker within that spiritual circle.

Its critique of greed is moral and poetic.

It does not accuse the medical profession as a whole, nor imply that charging for professional medical care is spiritually wrong.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Rooh padhta hoon,” “dua ka marham,” and “tasbeeh meri patti” are devotional metaphors.

Prayer, zikr, spiritual companionship, and compassion may support a person emotionally or spiritually, but they do not replace medical diagnosis, evidence-based treatment, medication, surgery, emergency care, or qualified clinical judgment.

Likewise, words attributed to Allah within the lyric are a literary device, not wahy, revelation, or literal Divine speech received by the writer.

Shifa is sought from Allah.
Medicine remains an entrusted means.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Meri Khamoshi Teri Saza Banegi | SufiPulse USA
description:
MERI KHAMOSHI TERI SAZA BANEGI
For Every Woman Silenced by Shame, Culture & Fear | A Sufi Reflection on Silence, Dignity & Justice

An original contemporary Sufi social reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

Meri Khamoshi Teri Saza Banegi begins where silence has been misunderstood.

A woman is hurt.
Society questions her.
The offender hides behind shame, custom, status, or sacred appearance.

“My silence will become your punishment.”

Not revenge.

Reckoning.

The silence once imposed upon the wounded becomes testimony, memory, conscience, and eventually voice.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

The composition speaks to women silenced by sexual violence, coercion, harassment, victim-blaming, fear, family pressure, workplace power, and social stigma.

Its questions are deliberate:

Why was she blamed for studying?
For working?
For being outside?
For what she wore?

Why was the scrutiny directed toward her before the person who harmed her?

The work places responsibility back upon the act of harm and the person responsible for it.

The woman at the center of this work is not defined only by what was done to her. She remains a moral agent whose dignity, voice, future, and right to be heard survive the violence.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

This is a Sufi protest against silence around abuse.

Its purpose is to confront victim-blaming, misuse of religious language, cultural excuses, and protection of perpetrators through silence.

“Sufism stands with the wounded” is the ethical position of this work.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Divine fire,” “Allah as witness,” “the mosque trembling,” “Makkah rejecting,” and punishment being written through tears are poetic and eschatological images.

They are not claims of new revelation, guaranteed Divine judgment against a named person, or permission for retaliation or violence.

Likewise, invoking Sayyida Zainab (RA) and Yazid is moral symbolism.

The composition does not claim that a contemporary survivor literally assumes Zainab’s historical station or that every offender is historically equivalent to Yazid.

The demand is accountability.

Not vengeance.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Woh Meri Kaaba Thi | Main Qibla Se Fisal Gaya | SufiPulse USA
description:
WOH MERI KAABA THI
Main Qibla Se Fisal Gaya | A Sufi Reflection on Mother, Qibla & Regret

A contemporary Sufi reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

Woh Meri Kaaba Thi begins as a confession.

A son looks back at the woman who carried him, fed him, prayed for him, endured for him — and realizes that while he learned how to face sacred directions, he failed to recognize the sacred responsibility inside his own home.

“Woh meri Kaaba thi — main Qibla se fisal gaya.”

The line is not theology.

It is regret.

The mother becomes the poem’s language for mercy, sacrifice, and the place to which the heart should have returned.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

The song is built around a painful contradiction.

A person may perform worship, repeat sacred words, visit sacred places, and still neglect the mother whose care made that life possible.

The composition places ritual beside responsibility.

What is outward devotion worth if gratitude fails at home?

The grief is not only that the mother is gone.

It is that understanding arrived after absence.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Kaaba,” “Qibla,” “Safa,” “Marwah,” “Arafah,” “Madina,” “Qur’an,” “Imam,” and similar sacred images are used poetically to describe maternal love, orientation, nurture, and moral memory.

They are not literal equivalences.

The Kaaba remains the Kaaba.
The Qibla remains the direction of prayer.
The Qur’an remains the revealed Book of Allah.
Prophethood belongs only to those whom Allah made prophets.

The metaphors express remorse, not a replacement of Islamic belief.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Some lines intentionally push devotional metaphor to its limit.

“Woh meri pehli Nabi thi,” “uski khamoshi Hadees thi,” “woh meri Qur’an thi,” or “woh meri Imam thi” should not be read literally.

A mother is not a prophet, revelation, scripture, qibla, or object of worship.

Likewise, “Arsh kaanp utha,” angels weeping, or sacred places rejecting the neglectful child are poetic images of conscience and accountability, not claims of witnessed unseen events.

The heart of the work is simpler:

honor your mother while she can still hear you.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Hu... Hu... | Har Girah Ki Kunji | SufiPulse USA
description:
HU... HU...
Har Girah Ki Kunji | A Sufi Reflection on Dhikr, Breath & the Key to Every Knot

An original contemporary Sufi mystical chant presented by SufiPulse USA.

Hu... Hu... begins with breath.

Before argument.
Before explanation.
Before the seeker finds language for what the heart is carrying.

In many Sufi traditions, “Hu” — “He” — is used in remembrance of Allah, drawing the seeker from multiplicity toward the One.

“Har girah ki kunji.”

The key to every knot.

Not because a syllable mechanically removes every difficulty, but because remembrance can change the heart with which difficulty is faced.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Some knots are external.

Others are tied within the self:

fear,
ego,
restlessness,
grief,
attachment,
and the inability to become still.

This composition uses repetition, breath, rhythm, silence, and zikr to create an inward movement from noise toward remembrance.

The chant does not promise escape from life.

It asks whether the seeker can return to Allah within it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Hu” is a pronoun meaning “He” in Arabic and has a long devotional presence within various Sufi traditions as an invocation referring to Allah.

Practices and interpretations of dhikr differ across Sufi communities.

This release presents a contemplative use of “Hu”; it does not claim that one form of remembrance is obligatory or universal.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“The Divine Name that opens every knot,” “Allah’s breath,” “Muhammad’s echo,” and the idea that each repetition dissolves another knot are poetic and mystical expressions.

They are not claims that breath is literally Divine, that Allah is contained in sound, or that repeating “Hu” guarantees healing, solutions, spiritual rank, or supernatural results.

Likewise, saying the lyrics were “revealed” is devotional language.

This work does not claim wahy, new revelation, Divine authorship, or infallibility.

The breath carries the zikr.
The zikr turns attention toward Allah.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
ZAMEEN BADLI, ROOH JUDA NAHIN HUI
I Left the Land, Not the Soul | A Kashmiri Sufi Reflection on Exile & Belonging

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Zameen Badli, Rooh Juda Nahin Hui begins with migration.

A Kashmiri soul walks through America while carrying a homeland that never fully became past tense.

The roads changed.
The skyline changed.

But memory remained.

“I left the land, not the soul.”

The song turns exile into a spiritual geography — where distance does not erase belonging, and where remembrance keeps walking beside the traveler.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Migration can relocate the body without relocating the inner world.

Brooklyn can suddenly become Naseembagh.
Seattle can whisper like Srinagar.
Arizona light can awaken the memory of Kashmir’s chinars.

It asks what happens when homeland survives not as possession, but as scent, sound, weather, language, prayer, and longing.

The journey becomes hijrat-e-rooh — a poetic migration of the soul.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

This work uses exile in an emotional and spiritual sense.

It does not claim that every migrant, immigrant, or member of a diaspora experiences displacement in the same way.

Nor does “hijrat-e-rooh” refer to a formal religious migration.

It is poetic language for the experience of carrying one landscape inside another.

It gives memory a voice.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The search for a “Wali” in America is presented as a spiritual and literary motif.

It does not claim that the writer received a guaranteed prophecy that a saint would appear, nor that an unknown person encountered in public should be assumed to possess spiritual rank.

Likewise, the idea that rivers become verses, mountains become prayers, or strangers become mirrors is poetic imagery.

The landscape does not issue revelation.

It awakens memory.

title: Shah-e-Hamdan Jaanta Hai Tu Kaun Hai | SufiPulse USA
description:
SHAH-E-HAMDAN JAANTA HAI TU KAUN HAI
Who Hijacked Kashmir’s Crafts? | A Sufi Indictment of Craft Exploitation

A contemporary Sufi social reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

Shah-e-Hamdan Jaanta Hai Tu Kaun Hai turns Kashmir’s craft economy into a moral courtroom.

The artisan stands at the center.

Not the trader.
Not the broker.
Not the brand.

The song asks what happens when the creating hand receives the smallest share, while others inherit the profit, prestige, and story.

“Shah-e-Hamdan jaanta hai tu kaun hai.”

This is not surveillance.

It is conscience.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Kashmir’s handicrafts carry generations of skill, memory, labor, and identity.

Yet craft value can be weakened when artisans lose bargaining power, provenance becomes opaque, imitation enters the market, or intermediaries capture disproportionate value.

This composition turns those concerns into spiritual accusation.

The question is not whether trade is wrong.

It is whether trade remains honorable when the maker becomes invisible.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Shah-e-Hamdan — Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani (RA) — occupies an important place in Kashmir’s religious memory.

Traditions often associate his influence and the wider movement around him with the transmission of crafts, skills, and cultural practices in Kashmir.

This song uses that remembered legacy symbolically.

It does not claim that every Kashmiri craft originated with one historical figure.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The “voice” or “knowledge” of Shah-e-Hamdan (RA) in this composition is poetic.

The work does not claim that a deceased saint literally identifies contemporary individuals, witnesses private commercial acts, or issues new judgments from the unseen.

Likewise, “middleman mafia,” “hijacked,” and “counterfeited” are protest language aimed at exploitative practices and systems.

They should not be read as criminal allegations against every intermediary, trader, exporter, institution, or unnamed person.

The indictment is ethical:

if value is created by the artisan, dignity must travel with the value.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Jawan-o-Kashmir Se | Khitab Qabl-e-Awliya | SufiPulse USA
description:
JAWAN-O-KASHMIR SE
Khitab Qabl-e-Awliya | A Sufi Call to the Youth of Kashmir

A contemporary Sufi reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

Jawan-o-Kashmir Se is addressed directly to Kashmir’s youth.

Not as an audience.

As inheritors.

The work places a generation before the memory of saints, poets, faqirs, and seekers who shaped Kashmir’s spiritual imagination.

Its question is simple:

What will you inherit — names, or character?

The anthem calls the young toward remembrance, courage, service, knowledge, conscience, and a spirituality strong enough to survive spectacle.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Kashmir carries an unusually dense spiritual memory.

Lal Ded.
Nund Rishi.
Shah-e-Hamdan.
Zain-ud-Din Wali.
Baba Rishi.
Makhdoom Sahib.
Dawood Khaki.
Shams Faqir.
Soch Kral.
Yaqub Sarfi.
Bulbul Shah.
And many others.

The song places their remembered lives before the next generation as questions of conduct.

If their names survive, what should survive through us?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The roll call of saints, poets, and spiritual figures is poetic and commemorative, not a complete historical genealogy or a claim that every figure belonged to one identical silsila.

“Before the saints rise” refers to memory becoming morally alive in a new generation.

It is not a claim that deceased saints literally return to direct contemporary affairs.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Several lines deliberately use intense Sufi metaphor.

“Our qibla is breath,” “our masjid is silence,” and “our imam is love” are poetic expressions. They do not replace the Kaaba as Qibla, the mosque as a place of worship, or the religious meaning of Imam.

“Ya Ali” is used within devotional Sufi language and does not attribute independent Divine power to Sayyiduna Ali (RA).

Statements such as “written by His Command” or “the heart was whispered to” are not claims of wahy, Divine authorship, or infallibility.

The call is inward:
inherit the fire without inventing authority.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
SUFI CRY FOR A RIVER
A Cry for the Jhelum | A Sufi Lament for the Jhelum and Kashmir’s Waters

A contemporary Sufi environmental reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

Sufi Cry for a River begins with Kashmir’s river as witness.

The Jhelum flows through landscape, settlement, memory, shrine, livelihood, and history.

In this work, the river is given a voice.

Not because water literally speaks.

Because what happens to a river tells us something about the people living beside it.

“When the Jhelum cries, Kashmir must listen.”

The cry is ecological.
The reckoning is human.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

The Jhelum is more than scenery.

It supports communities, ecosystems, cultural memory, and generations of life across Kashmir.

Pollution, unmanaged waste, sewage, encroachment, and neglect are therefore not only environmental problems.

They become questions of responsibility.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The composition uses Kashmir’s Sufi geography poetically, imagining shrines, saints, settlements, and the Jhelum as parts of a remembered spiritual landscape.

It does not claim that saints literally communicated through the river or that every shrine along the Jhelum belonged to one historical silsila.

Water carries memory in the poem.
History requires evidence.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

References to the Jhelum “crying,” saints “speaking,” or the river “testifying” are poetic personification.

Likewise, the 2014 Kashmir flood may be contemplated spiritually by a believer, but this work does not claim scientific authority to declare it a direct Divine message or punishment.

Floods have hydrological, climatic, infrastructural, and land-use dimensions requiring scientific analysis.

Spiritual reflection asks another question:

What did we learn after the water receded?

The song calls for repentance expressed through action, not fear.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Shah-e-Hamdan Returns | SufiPulse USA
description:
SHAH-E-HAMDAN RETURNS
Kashmir’s Sacred Crafts Are Under Attack | A Sufi Indictment of Fake Kashmir Crafts

A contemporary Sufi social reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

Shah-e-Hamdan Returns imagines Kashmir’s craft inheritance standing up to examine the marketplace built around it.

The saint does not literally return.

Conscience does.

The work turns toward counterfeit goods, misleading origin claims, machine-made substitutes, opaque middlemen, and the distance between the artisan and the market.

“Shah-e-Hamdan walks again.”

In the poem, the inheritance begins asking questions.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Kashmir’s handmade traditions carry skill, memory, livelihood, and cultural identity.

When imitation is sold as handmade, when provenance is hidden, or when the maker disappears behind layers of trade, the damage exceeds one transaction.

Trust erodes.
Artisans lose leverage.
Heritage becomes branding without accountability.

This song asks who benefits when authenticity becomes difficult to see.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Shah-e-Hamdan — Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani (RA) — holds an important place in Kashmir’s spiritual memory.

Traditions also associate his influence with crafts, skills, and cultural practices.

This composition uses that remembered legacy symbolically.

It does not claim that every Kashmiri craft originated with Shah-e-Hamdan or that one figure alone created Kashmir’s craft economy.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Shah-e-Hamdan Returns” is a poetic device.

The work does not claim that Shah-e-Hamdan (RA) literally returns, identifies contemporary offenders, witnesses commercial acts from the unseen, or issues new judgments.

Terms such as “middleman veil,” “theft,” and “counterfeit” are protest language directed toward deceptive practices and systems.

They are not criminal allegations against every trader, exporter, intermediary, or unnamed person.

The moral test is simple:

If something is sold as authentic Kashmir craft, can its origin, process, and maker withstand scrutiny?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
MIRROR OF HAZRATBAL, WOUND OF DAL
Hazratbal Still Shines, But Dal Lake Bleeds | A Kashmiri Scientist in Exile Weeps for Dal Lake

An original contemporary Sufi environmental reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Mirror of Hazratbal, Wound of Dal begins with a reflection.

Hazratbal still stands in light.

Dal Lake carries the wound.

The song places sacred memory beside ecological decline and asks what it means to revere a place spiritually while allowing the waters beside it to deteriorate.

“The Dal. The Dal. The lake of name.”

The lake becomes mirror, memory, and warning.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Dal Lake is not only an image of Kashmir.

It is a living ecological system shaped by hydrology, settlement, waste, nutrient loading, land-use pressure, and decades of intervention.

For the writer, it is also personal.

A lake once studied through environmental science and remote sensing now returns through exile as grief.

The distance sharpens the question:

What did we preserve in memory that we failed to protect in reality?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The composition places Hazratbal and Dal Lake beside one another as spiritual and ecological symbols.

Hazratbal is not blamed for the lake’s condition, nor is religious devotion presented as an environmental management strategy.

A sacred landscape can remain revered while the ecosystem surrounding it continues to suffer.

Faith does not replace restoration.

It can deepen responsibility toward it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Dal Lake bleeds,” “the lake speaks,” and similar expressions are poetic personification.

They do not mean the lake literally suffers as a human being.

The writer’s grief as a Kashmiri environmental scientist in exile is personal testimony, not a substitute for water-quality data, ecological monitoring, or institutional assessment.

Spiritual language carries the lament.

Science must still measure the wound.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Needle’s Hell to Noor’s Bright Dawn | SufiPulse USA
description:
NEEDLE’S HELL TO NOOR’S BRIGHT DAWN
From Heroin to Divine Light | A Drug-Free Kashmir Sufi Anthem

A Sufi recovery reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Needle’s Hell to Noor’s Bright Dawn begins inside addiction.

Not as spectacle.
Not as moral failure.

As pain.

The work follows a Kashmiri young person through dependence, withdrawal, isolation, stigma, and recovery.

Dr. Zarf-e-Noori witnessed this seeker’s three-year journey around the darbar of Dr. Ghulam Mohammad Kumar of Ganderbal — Kumar Sahib.

“From needle’s hell to Noor’s bright dawn.”

The light is metaphor.
Recovery is work.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This anthem refuses to reduce a person to the substance they used.

The song comes from witnessed proximity, not abstract commentary.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

This work was inspired by the recovery journey of a Sufi seeker known personally to Dr. Zarf-e-Noori.

His identity is intentionally withheld.

For about three years, the writer witnessed his struggle and recovery around Dr. Kumar’s darbar, where both were seekers under the same Murshid.

That witness is personal and spiritual, not a clinical case record.

Spiritual companionship should not be read as evidence that spiritual intervention alone treats opioid or heroin dependence.

Recovery may involve medical care, counseling, medication, rehabilitation, and social support.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Unknown Sufi Seeker” does not mean unknown to the writer.

It means his identity is private.

Dr. Zarf-e-Noori wrote and conceptualized this work after witnessing approximately three years of this seeker’s journey at Dr. Kumar’s darbar.

They were fellow seekers under the same Sufi master — spiritual brothers on the path.

The writer watched struggle, return, companionship, and gradual change unfold before him.

“Needle’s hell,” “Noor’s bright dawn,” and “Divine transformation” are poetic expressions.

They do not mean addiction is punishment from Allah, that relapse reflects weak faith, or that prayer replaces evidence-based treatment.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
ALLAH IN THE ALGORITHM
Can the Divine Be Found in Code? | A Sufi Reflection on AI, Code & Divine Presence

An original contemporary Sufi-tech reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Allah in the Algorithm enters the digital world with an old question:

Can technology deepen remembrance without becoming an idol of its own?

From GIS maps and remote sensing to software, climate systems, infrastructure, and artificial intelligence, the song follows a modern seeker moving between code and contemplation.

“Allah in the algorithm” is not a technical claim.

It is a metaphor for seeing order, responsibility, and meaning within systems built by human hands.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This work asks whether screens, data, models, code, and networks can still become places of ethical attention.

A map can reveal vulnerability.
A sensor can detect change.
An algorithm can organize information.
A warning system can protect life.

The spiritual question is what the human being does with that capacity.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Allah in the Algorithm” does not mean Allah is contained inside software, artificial intelligence, mathematics, data, or computational systems.

Algorithms are human-designed procedures.

AI systems are technologies, not Divine agents and not sources of revelation.

The composition uses technical language as metaphor for awe, responsibility, uncertainty, and the limits of human control.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Lines such as “Allah writes the algorithm behind every raindrop,” “remote sensing as Divine observation,” or “code for Allah” are poetic expressions.

They are not scientific propositions.

Rainfall follows physical processes that can be observed and modeled. Remote sensing measures signals through instruments. Software executes instructions.

Faith enters at another level: meaning, intention, stewardship, humility, and accountability.

Science measures the system.
The seeker asks what responsibility follows.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

NEW AGE SUFI ON HIGHWAY TO HAQQ
Finding God in a Modern World | A Modern Sufi Journey Toward Truth

A contemporary Sufi travel reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

New Age Sufi on Highway to Haqq begins on the road.

Across American highways, cities, weather, and long stretches of solitude, a Kashmiri seeker carries two maps:

the map outside,
and the map within.

“Highway to Haqq.”

The phrase is not about reaching Allah through geography.

It is about what the traveler becomes while moving through the world.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Modern life is full of movement.

Work.
Data.
Traffic.
Deadlines.
Storm alerts.
Screens.
Miles.

The song asks whether a seeker can remain spiritually awake inside that speed.

For an environmental scientist and emergency planner, the road is more than scenery.

It is infrastructure, risk, climate, landscape, and human vulnerability.

But beneath all of that remains another question:

Where is the heart going?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Highway to Haqq” is a contemporary Sufi metaphor.

Haqq refers to Truth and, in Islamic devotional language, to Allah as al-Haqq — The Truth.

Travel, technology, science, or professional work do not automatically produce spiritual realization.

The highway is an image of movement; the spiritual journey still requires intention, discipline, remembrance, and responsibility.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Finding God in a modern world” does not mean Allah is physically located in highways, landscapes, technology, or human systems.

Travel becomes a contemplative frame.

Likewise, terms such as “emergency seeker,” “remote sensing soul,” and “environmental Sufi” are poetic identities, not religious ranks.

Science observes the world.
Emergency planning prepares for disruption.

The seeker asks what all that knowledge does to the self.

The road provides distance.
Zikr provides orientation.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Cry of the Kashmir Valley | Come Light the Mystic Lamp | SufiPulse USA
description:
CRY OF THE KASHMIR VALLEY
Come Light the Mystic Lamp | A Mystic Rap-Rock Uprising for Kashmir’s Sufi Soul

A contemporary Kashmiri Sufi reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

Cry of the Kashmir Valley begins with a question:

What happens when a culture remembers the names of its saints but loses the compassion, zikr, poetry, music, hospitality, and inner discipline associated with them?

“Come light the lamp.”

The lamp is memory.
The flame is responsibility.

It asks whether Kashmir’s inherited spiritual imagination still has something to say to the present.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Kashmir carries a deep and diverse spiritual inheritance.

Lal Ded.
Nund Rishi.
Shah-e-Hamdan.
Makhdoom Sahib.
And generations of poets, faqirs, teachers, women, artisans, and seekers.

Its concern is what happens when spiritual inheritance becomes slogan without ethics.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

This anthem responds to tensions around Kashmir’s Sufi heritage, including debates over shrines, devotional music, zikr, local custom, and religious identity.

It does not declare any Muslim community outside Islam, nor treat every reformist, Salafi, or conservative interpretation as hostile to Kashmir.

The critique is directed at intolerance, erasure, coercion, and contempt for inherited spiritual culture wherever those behaviors appear.

The song argues for memory without sectarian hatred.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“The saints speak,” “the Valley cries,” “the lamp returns,” and references to Dr. Kumar’s unseen fire are poetic expressions.

They do not mean deceased saints literally speak through the recording, return to direct contemporary affairs, or transmit new revelation.

Likewise, the work’s language of uprising is spiritual and cultural.

It is not a call to violence.

The rebellion is against forgetting.
The resistance is remembrance.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Let Mansur Speak | SufiPulse USA
description:
LET MANSUR SPEAK
The Voice That Cried Ana al-Haqq | A Sufi Reflection on Mansur al-Hallaj, Truth & Sacrifice

A contemporary Sufi reflection presented by SufiPulse USA.

Let Mansur Speak turns toward Husayn ibn Mansur al-Hallaj — the 10th-century mystic whose name remains inseparable from the cry:

“Ana al-Haqq.”

I am the Truth.

The phrase still burns where mystical language, theology, authority, and love collide.

This work asks why some words continue to burn long after the speaker is gone.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Al-Hallaj has been remembered as mystic, poet, controversial teacher, ecstatic lover, condemned heretic, and martyr of spiritual truth — depending on the tradition interpreting him.

What happens when inward experience becomes public speech?

What happens when spiritual language is heard by institutions that understand it differently?

What price can truth carry when conviction refuses silence?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Mansur al-Hallaj was executed in Baghdad in 922 CE after a complex process involving religious, political, and legal factors.

It is too simple to say he was executed only because he uttered “Ana al-Haqq.”

Many later Sufi readings understand the phrase through fanā — the effacement of ego before Divine Reality — rather than as a literal claim that al-Hallaj was God.

This release presents that devotional reading without declaring it the only one.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Let Mansur Speak” is poetic resurrection, not literal return.

Descriptions of al-Hallaj as “the voice of God,” of his words as prophecy, or of mystical truth as automatically superior to religious scholarship are not doctrinal claims.

Allah alone is Divine.

A human being does not become Allah through mystical experience.

Fanā here means self-effacement and surrender — not identity with God.

The fire is metaphor.
The sacrifice is historical.
The question remains alive.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Sultan | The Spiritual King of Kashmir | SufiPulse USA
description:
SULTAN
The Spiritual King of Kashmir | A Sufi Tribute to Sheikh Hamza Makhdoom Kashmiri (RA)

An original contemporary Sufi tribute by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Sultan turns toward Sheikh Hamza Makhdoom Kashmiri (RA) — Makhdoom Sahib — as one of Kashmir’s enduring spiritual presences.

The song does not imagine a worldly throne.

It imagines an inward one.

A hidden throne of light.
A gate of discipline.
A station where the seeker confronts what still stands between the self and Allah.

“Sultan.”

Not sovereign over Kashmir.

A spiritual king in the language of devotion.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This work approaches Makhdoom Sahib through Kashmir’s inherited memory of sanctity, discipline, spiritual authority, and inward transformation.

The title “Sultan” is not about political power.

It asks what spiritual authority looks like without palace, army, or worldly office.

A saint is remembered not by what he possessed, but by what his remembrance continues to awaken.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“The Spiritual King of Kashmir” is a devotional and poetic title used within this composition.

It is not a claim of political sovereignty, formal jurisdiction over Kashmiri Muslims, or supremacy over every saint, scholar, or Sufi lineage.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Divine authority,” “inner gatekeeping,” “hidden throne of light,” and the idea that a seeker must “pass through” the saint are mystical metaphors.

They do not mean Makhdoom Sahib possesses Allah’s authority, controls Divine decree, knows the unseen independently, or stands between Allah and a believer in an absolute theological sense.

Allah alone possesses sovereignty and knowledge of the unseen.

The saint is honored as guide, memory, and spiritual mirror.

Love intensifies the language.
Tawheed preserves the boundary.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Dr. Kumar Faqeer | Kashmir Calling Me | SufiPulse USA
description:
DR. KUMAR FAQEER
Kashmir Calling Me | From Physician to Qalandar-e-Zaman

An original contemporary Sufi tribute by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Kashmir Calling Me begins with a summons.

Not from a map.
Not from nostalgia.

From a spiritual pull that would not leave the seeker alone.

The song turns toward Dr. Ghulam Mohammad Kumar of Ganderbal — Kumar Sahib, Mama Ji, Dr. Kumar Faqeer — whose life and presence became a decisive force in Dr. Zarf-e-Noori’s spiritual journey.

“Kashmir calling me.”

The geography becomes inward.

The destination becomes the Murshid.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

This work traces a movement from profession to surrender, scientific training to spiritual questioning, and distance to discipleship.

Dr. Kumar is remembered here as a physician who stepped away from conventional professional life and entered a long period of withdrawal, silence, and inner discipline before returning to spiritual guidance.

The song asks what happens when knowledge reaches the edge of what it can measure.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Qalandar-e-Zaman,” “Dr. Kumar Faqeer,” and similar titles are devotional descriptions used by followers and within this creative tradition.

They are not official religious offices or empirically verifiable spiritual ranks.

description:
SEEKER TO SUFI
Divine Homecoming | A Journey From Searching to Divine Homecoming

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Seeker to Sufi begins with exhaustion.

The seeker has searched through identities, distance, ambition, and the need to arrive somewhere.

Then the direction changes.

Not outward.

Inward.

“No more seeking, no more plea... I am finally a Sufi.”

The line is not a declaration of spiritual rank.

It is the relief of a seeker who finally recognizes the path he wants to walk.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Some journeys do not end because every question has been answered.

They end because the seeker discovers how to live inside the question.

This work moves through surrender, zikr, silence, inner freedom, Divine love, and the loosening of identities built only for the outer world.

The homecoming is not to a place.

It is to orientation.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“I am finally a Sufi” is personal and poetic language.

It does not claim sainthood, spiritual completion, formal Sufi initiation, or superiority over other Muslims or religious paths.

Sufism is presented here as an inward discipline of remembrance, humility, service, and love within the writer’s Islamic framework.

Arrival does not mean the journey is finished.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

The phrases “found the Truth within,” “Divine homecoming,” and “looked within and found everything” are mystical expressions.

They do not mean that Allah is physically contained inside the human being or that inward feeling replaces revelation, ethics, prayer, or religious responsibility.

Likewise, “beyond rituals, robes, or religions” should not be read as rejection of religious practice or doctrine.

The point is simpler:

external form without inner transformation is incomplete.

The seeker comes home not by becoming Divine, but by becoming more surrendered to Allah.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: I Am a Sinner | Yet You Whisper Inside | SufiPulse USA
description:
I AM A SINNER
Yet You Whisper Inside | A Sufi Reflection on Sin, Mercy & the Voice Within

An original contemporary Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

I Am a Sinner begins with confession.

Not performance.
Not self-condemnation.

Confession.

The seeker stands before Allah with failure, regret, longing, and the fear that he has gone too far to return.

Then comes the whisper:

“You are not the sin — you are the seeker.”

The line does not erase responsibility.

It opens the door to mercy.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Sin can distort how a person sees himself.

The seeker may begin to confuse what he has done with what he is.

This work separates accountability from despair.

A person can regret.
A person can repent.
A person can return.

The song asks whether shame should become a wall between the seeker and Allah — or whether remorse can become the first step back.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

The “Divine whisper” in this composition is a literary and devotional device.

It represents the seeker’s inward experience of mercy, Qur’anic hope, remembrance, and conscience.

It is not presented as literal new speech from Allah, private revelation, or a claim that the writer received words outside revelation.

The dialogue is poetic.

The mercy it seeks is theological.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Yet You whisper inside,” “Your voice lives within me,” and similar lines should not be read as saying Allah physically inhabits the human being.

Within Islamic belief, Allah is not contained by the body, mind, heart, or created space.

The “voice within” is poetic language for conscience, remembrance, hope, and the inward pull toward repentance.

Likewise, “you are not the sin” does not mean actions have no consequences.

Mercy does not cancel accountability.

It makes return possible.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: O Shah-e-Hamdan | We Owe You All, Our Roots, Our Way | SufiPulse USA
description:
O SHAH-E-HAMDAN
We Owe You All, Our Roots, Our Way | A Sufi Tribute to Kashmir’s Spiritual & Craft Legacy

A contemporary Sufi tribute presented by SufiPulse USA.

O Shah-e-Hamdan turns toward Amir-e-Kabir Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani (RA) as one of the most powerful remembered influences on Kashmir’s spiritual, ethical, and craft history.

“He brought no sword, but soul.
No empire, but ethics.
No map, but meaning.”

The language is devotional.
The gratitude is civilizational.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

For generations, Shah-e-Hamdan (RA) has occupied a central place in Kashmir’s religious memory.

Traditions associate his influence, and that of the wider movement around him, with spiritual teaching, scholarship, social ethics, crafts, skills, and cultural exchange.

If Kashmir remembers Shah-e-Hamdan, what should it protect?

Faith.
Dignity.
Craft.
Service.
Honest work.
Memory.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Kashmir owes you its crafts, faith & way” is devotional and poetic framing.

It should not be read as a claim that Kashmir had no spiritual, artistic, or craft traditions before Shah-e-Hamdan (RA), or that one historical figure alone created Kashmir’s religious and craft identity.

This composition honors Shah-e-Hamdan’s remembered contribution within that larger history.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Statements such as “Kashmir rose from his footsteps,” “soul architect of Kashmir,” or that the song was “received rather than written” are poetic expressions.

They are not claims of wahy, Divine authorship, infallibility, or supernatural historical authority.

Reverence for Shah-e-Hamdan (RA) does not make him an object of worship or assign him independent Divine power.

Allah alone is worshipped.

The saint is remembered through influence, service, scholarship, ethics, and love.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: I Am Sufi, I Am You | Interfaith Sufi Song | SufiPulse USA
description:
I AM SUFI, I AM YOU
Beyond Religion, Race & Borders | A Sufi Anthem for Interfaith & Human Unity

An original contemporary interfaith Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

I Am Sufi, I Am You begins with a refusal to make difference an excuse for distance.

Moses.
Jesus.
Muhammad ﷺ.

Three prophetic names.
Three sacred histories.
One call to remember that reverence does not require contempt for another.

“I am not other.
I am you.”

The line is not about erasing identity.

It is about refusing dehumanization.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Religion can become a bridge or a boundary depending on what human beings do with it.

This composition turns toward the Abrahamic prophetic memory through a Sufi language of humility, love, recognition, and shared human dignity.

It asks whether a believer can remain rooted in faith while still seeing the neighbor, stranger, refugee, outsider, or person of another religion as fully human.

The answer of the song is yes.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Beyond religion, race & borders” is poetic language for human solidarity.

It does not mean religions are doctrinally identical, that theological differences are irrelevant, or that SufiPulse claims one universal creed for everyone.

Likewise, moving from Sinai to Nazareth to Medina is a symbolic journey through prophetic memory.

The work honors difference while rejecting hatred.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“I carry all Prophets in one breath,” “one Truth under many names,” and “I am you” are devotional and interfaith metaphors.

They should not be read as saying every religion teaches the same theology, that all distinctions between prophets disappear, or that the human being becomes Divine.

Within the writer’s Islamic framework, Allah remains One, and the prophets remain His messengers.

The work invites recognition without theological erasure.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

description:
DR. GHULAM MOHAMMAD KUMAR FAQEER
Physician, Qalandar & Sufi Legend of Kashmir | A Tribute to the Mystic of Ganderbal

An original contemporary Sufi tribute by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This work turns toward Dr. Ghulam Mohammad Kumar of Ganderbal — Kumar Sahib, Mama Ji, Dr. Kumar Faqeer — as physician, seeker, Murshid, and Qalandar in the devotional memory of those formed around him.

The song follows a movement:

from medicine to silence,
from profession to retreat,
from healing bodies to transforming seekers,
from visibility to hiddenness.

“Dr. Kumar – Sufi Legend.”

Not a title of worldly fame.

A disciple’s language for a life that chose surrender over recognition.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Some spiritual lives are remembered through books.

Others through what changes in the people who encountered them.

This composition approaches Dr. Kumar through the second path.

His quiet presence, withdrawal from worldly ambition, forest solitude, disciplined silence, and return to spiritual guidance became part of the inner history of those who came to him.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“Qalandar-e-Zaman,” “Sufi Legend of Kashmir,” “hidden saint,” and similar descriptions are devotional titles used within this creative tradition.

They are not official religious offices, empirically established spiritual ranks, or claims that one person stands above every saint or Sufi lineage of Kashmir.

The work presents Dr. Kumar through the testimony of disciples and seekers.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

Phrases such as “radiant spiritual depth,” “God’s hidden radiance,” or that a Murshid transforms through silence are mystical expressions.

They do not mean Dr. Kumar possesses Divine attributes, controls the unseen, or operates independently of Allah.

Fanā refers here to the Sufi language of diminishing ego before Allah.

The tribute is devotional testimony, not a claim of revelation, infallibility, or supernatural proof.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: I Am Kashmiri Sufi | The Saints Still Walk | SufiPulse USA
description:
I AM KASHMIRI SUFI
The Saints Still Walk | A Sufi Anthem of Memory, Identity & Living Inheritance

A contemporary Kashmiri Sufi reflection by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

I Am Kashmiri Sufi begins as a declaration of spiritual identity.

Not an argument.
Not a border.
Not a claim of superiority.

A remembrance.

The song turns toward Kashmir as Reshiwar — a landscape shaped by saints, poets, faqirs, zikr, silence, service, and resistance to forgetting.

“The saints still walk.”

Not literally.

They walk through what remains alive in us.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Lal Ded.
Nund Rishi.
Zain-ud-Din Wali.
And generations of seekers whose names and ethical memory still inhabit the Valley.

This anthem asks whether inheritance can survive without imitation.

To call oneself a Kashmiri Sufi is not merely to inherit names.

It is to inherit questions:

How do you treat the weak?
What do you do with power?
Can memory become service?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

“The Saints Still Walk” is poetic language for living cultural and spiritual influence.

It does not claim that deceased saints physically walk among people, direct contemporary affairs, or communicate new revelation.

Likewise, “Sufi uprising,” “war cry,” and “march” describe cultural and spiritual intensity.

They are not calls to violence.

The resistance is against erasure, hatred, and forgetfulness.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Reshiwar” is invoked as a cultural-spiritual image of Kashmir, not as proof that every Kashmiri shares one religious identity or one interpretation of history.

Lal Ded, Nund Rishi, Zain-ud-Din Wali, and other figures belong to distinct historical contexts.

The song gathers them poetically without erasing those differences.

Spiritual inheritance becomes meaningful only when memory becomes conduct.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Kemis Taani Chhu Aav Aav | A Kashmiri-English Sufi Kalam | SufiPulse USA
description:
KEMIS TAANI CHHU AAV AAV
A Kashmiri-English Sufi Kalam

An original contemporary Sufi kalam by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

Kemis Taani Chhu Aav Aav is built around a call rather than an explanation.

“Kemis taani chhu aav aav.”

For whom has the presence arrived?
For whom does the call come?

The composition does not answer for the listener. It turns the listener inward.

Its English passages open the meaning, while two adopted Kashmiri verses associated with Mahjoor preserve the sound, rhythm, and spiritual weight of the Kashmiri source tradition.

The Kashmiri lines are not ornamental. They are the spiritual anchor of the work.

The English verses open the meaning.
The Kashmiri verses carry the presence.

Words begin to fall away.
Silence begins to speak.
The seeker begins to listen.

The call you hear is not outside.
It is rising from within.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

SufiPulse USA creates sacred media for remembrance, reflection, and awakening.

This work was shaped for listeners who may not speak Kashmiri but still seek its spiritual and emotional world.

Rather than translate everything into English, Kashmiri and English coexist.

One language explains.
The other remembers.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

Two verses from Mahjoor’s kalam are retained because their cadence and cultural memory carry something translation alone cannot reproduce.

They are not decoration. They form the point of return for the contemporary English composition.

Adaptation should acknowledge lineage rather than erase it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Bulbul chhu baraan” is acknowledged as adopted material from Mahjoor’s poetic tradition.

The contemporary English composition, framing, and interpretive journey are by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori.

The purpose is not to claim inherited poetry, but to carry its living sound into a new linguistic setting.

The call remains Kashmiri.
The listening becomes universal.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Phir Likh Zarf-e-Noori | Faith Does Not Fear Critics | SufiPulse USA
description:
PHIR LIKH ZARF-E-NOORI
Faith Does Not Fear Critics

An original contemporary Sufi expression by Dr. Zarf-e-Noori, presented by SufiPulse USA.

This is not just a song.
It is a rebuttal.

After a month of silence, the expression returns — not as reaction, but as clarity.

Grammar was questioned.
Music was questioned.
Sufi meaning was questioned.
Even the right to express was questioned.

Dr. Zarf-e-Noori has no formal training in Urdu. Yet the words arrived in Urdu. The expression did not wait for academic permission.

Thought became pressure.
Pressure became language.
Language became song again.

The real discomfort was not that the work answered criticism.

It was that the expression continued without permission.

“Jo likhwaata hai woh jaane.”

The One who makes it written knows.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WHY THIS WORK

Phir Likh asks whether expression must first satisfy gatekeepers before it is allowed to exist.

Its answer is not argument.

It is continuation.

Faith does not fear critics.
Depth does not weaken it.
Expression does not break it.
Sincerity does not threaten it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ EDITORIAL NOTE

This release emerged after criticism of language, music, Sufi interpretation, and authorship.

Rather than answer every objection individually, the work chooses a different response:

Write again.

Critique can sharpen language and deepen thought. But criticism and permission are not the same thing.

A creator may listen carefully without surrendering the right to continue creating.

“You bring words. I bring fire.”

Continuation with conviction.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

◆ WRITER’S NOTE

“Jo likhwaata hai woh jaane” is devotional language, not a claim that every line carries Divine authority or is beyond correction.

The writer distinguishes inspiration from revelation.

The work expresses the experience of language arriving with unusual force despite the absence of formal Urdu training. It is presented poetically and personally.

Faith does not require intellectual immunity. Sincere expression can remain open to correction.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
